Given the lack of efficacy of aspirin in AF, it is important that this lady is commenced on anticoagulation as a priority to reduce the risk of further stroke in the interim. The CT head has ruled out intra-cranial haemorrhage, and therefore this TIA is likely a cardio-embolic phenomenon for which anticoagulation is more efficacious than aspirin.

Non-urgent referral to the TIA clinic
In view of her ABCD2 score, she will require referral to the TIA clinic. The presence of AF is independently considered to place the patient in the high-risk category, and will, therefore, necessitate urgent referral to the TIA clinic. Her CHADS-VASC score will necessitate anti-coagulation.

Refer the patient to psychiatry
Clearly, a psychiatric referral is inappropriate.

stem: Which one of the following treatments is not appropriate in the management of Wolff-Parkinson White?
options: Radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway
explanation:
Verapamil
The correct answer is Verapamil, as it is contraindicated in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome. Verapamil, a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, can be dangerous in patients with WPW as it blocks conduction through the AV node while having no effect on conduction through the accessory pathway. This can result in preferential conduction down the accessory pathway, potentially precipitating ventricular fibrillation in patients with atrial fibrillation and WPW.

Sotalol
Sotalol is an appropriate treatment option for WPW. It is a Class III antiarrhythmic drug with additional beta-blocking properties. It prolongs the refractory period of both the normal conducting system and the accessory pathway, making it effective in preventing re-entrant tachycardias.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is also an appropriate treatment for WPW. As a Class III antiarrhythmic drug, it prolongs the action potential duration and refractory period in all cardiac tissue, including both the normal conducting system and the accessory pathway. It is particularly useful in acute situations and in patients with structural heart disease.

Flecainide
Flecainide, a Class IC antiarrhythmic drug, is an appropriate option for WPW. It works by slowing conduction through both the normal pathway and the accessory pathway, helping to prevent re-entrant tachycardias. It is particularly useful in patients without structural heart disease.

Radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway
Radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway is considered the definitive treatment for WPW syndrome. It offers a potential cure by destroying the abnormal conducting tissue that causes the preexcitation. It has a high success rate and is the treatment of choice, particularly in young patients or those with frequent symptomatic episodes.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is incorrect?
options: Stent thrombosis usually occurs in the first month
Restenosis is more common than stent thrombosis
Around 95% of patients have a stent fitted during a PCI
Renal impairment is a risk factor for restenosis
Patients with drug-eluting stents require a shorter duration of clopidogrel therapy
explanation:
Patients with drug-eluting stents require a shorter duration of clopidogrel therapy
PCI - patients with drug-eluting stents require a longer duration of clopidogrel therapy. The correct answer is 'Patients with drug-eluting stents require a shorter duration of clopidogrel therapy'. This statement is incorrect. According to the UK guidelines, patients who have been fitted with drug-eluting stents should receive dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), which includes aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel, for at least 6 months to prevent stent thrombosis. In some cases, depending on the patient's risk factors and tolerance, DAPT may be extended beyond 6 months.

Stent thrombosis usually occurs in the first month
Stent thrombosis usually occurs in the first month' - This statement is true. Stent thrombosis is a serious complication of PCI that can lead to myocardial infarction or death. It most commonly occurs within the first month after the procedure, especially if there's premature discontinuation of antiplatelet therapy.

Restenosis is more common than stent thrombosis
Restenosis is more common than stent thrombosis' - This statement is also correct. Restenosis, or the re-narrowing of the artery after PCI, happens more frequently than stent thrombosis. While advancements in stent technology have reduced its incidence, it still occurs in around 10-20% of cases within 6-9 months post-procedure.

Around 95% of patients have a stent fitted during a PCI
Around 95% of patients have a stent fitted during a PCI' - This option is accurate too. The vast majority of PCIs involve placing a stent in the affected coronary artery to help keep it open and improve blood flow to the heart.

Renal impairment is a risk factor for restenosis
Renal impairment is a risk factor for restenosis' - Lastly, this statement is true as well. Patients with renal impairment have been found to have higher rates of restenosis after PCI due to factors like increased platelet aggregation and inflammation.

stem: A 60-year-old male has a past medical history of hypertension, type II diabetes and ischaemic heart disease. He has recently been started on a new medication. His GP notices that his HbA1c has increased significantly over the same period. Which medication is most likely to have adversely affected his glycaemic control?
explanation:
Bendroflumethiazide
Thiazides can worsen glucose tolerance. The correct answer is bendroflumethiazide. Thiazides can worsen glycaemic control and increase urate levels which can worsen gout.

Alendronic acid
The other drugs are not known to have an effect on glycaemic control.

Amiodarone
The other drugs are not known to have an effect on glycaemic control.

Allopurinol
The other drugs are not known to have an effect on glycaemic control.

Calcium carbonate and vitamin D3
The other drugs are not known to have an effect on glycaemic control.

stem: What is the role of troponin in cardiac muscle?
options: Acts as a lining of the T tubules
Anchors thick and thin filaments together
explanation:
Component of the thin filaments
The correct answer is that troponin is a component of the thin filaments. Troponin is a complex of three regulatory proteins (troponin C, troponin I, and troponin T) that is integral to muscle contraction in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Located on the actin filament, troponin works in conjunction with tropomyosin to regulate the interaction between actin and myosin. When calcium binds to troponin C, it causes a conformational change that moves tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge formation and muscle contraction.

Component of the thick filaments
Component of the thick filaments is incorrect because thick filaments are primarily composed of myosin molecules. Myosin has a tail region that forms the backbone of the thick filament and globular heads that extend outward to interact with actin during muscle contraction.

Acts as a lining of the T tubules
Acts as a lining of the T tubules is incorrect. T tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that conduct action potentials into the interior of the muscle fibre. They are lined by the cell membrane and do not contain troponin.

Anchors thick filament to Z-discs
Anchors thick filament to Z-discs is incorrect. This is actually the role of titin, a giant elastic protein that connects the M-line to the Z-disc and helps maintain sarcomere structure and provides elasticity to muscle fibres.

Anchors thick and thin filaments together
Anchors thick and thin filaments together is incorrect. While troponin is involved in regulating the interaction between thick and thin filaments during contraction, it does not serve as a permanent anchor between them. The interaction between thick and thin filaments is dynamic and regulated by calcium levels and ATP availability.

stem: Where is the site of action of bendroflumethiazide?
options: Proximal part of the distal convoluted tubules
Distal part of the distal convoluted tubules
explanation:
Proximal part of the distal convoluted tubules
Thiazides/thiazide-like drugs (e.g. indapamide) - inhibits sodium reabsorption by blocking the Na+-Clˆ’ symporter at the beginning of the distal convoluted tubule. The correct answer is that bendroflumethiazide acts at the proximal part of the distal convoluted tubules. Thiazide diuretics, including bendroflumethiazide, work by inhibiting the sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC) in the early portion of the distal convoluted tubule. This results in decreased sodium and chloride reabsorption, leading to increased sodium and water excretion. Additionally, thiazides increase calcium reabsorption, making them useful in treating conditions like hypercalciuria and osteoporosis.

Proximal convoluted tubules
Proximal convoluted tubules is incorrect. While this segment is responsible for reabsorbing approximately 65% of filtered sodium, it is not the site of action for thiazide diuretics. Loop diuretics and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (like acetazolamide) act here, but not thiazides.

Ascending loop of Henle
Ascending loop of Henle is incorrect. This is the site of action for loop diuretics such as furosemide, which inhibit the sodium-potassiumchloride cotransporter (NKCC2). Loop diuretics are more potent than thiazides because of their location and mechanism of action.

Descending loop of Henle
Descending loop of Henle is incorrect. This segment is primarily involved in water reabsorption through aquaporin channels and is not a target for any major diuretic medications.

Distal part of the distal convoluted tubules
Distal part of the distal convoluted tubules is incorrect. While this segment is involved in sodium reabsorption through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), it is the target for potassium-sparing diuretics like amiloride and triamterene, not thiazides.

stem: A 54-year-old man with atypical chest pain is referred to cardiology. An exercise ECG shows non-specific ST and T wave changes. Following this an coronary angiogram is performed which demonstrates no evidence of atherosclerosis. A diagnosis of Prinzmetal's angina is suspected. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
explanation:
Felodipine
Prinzmetal angina - treatment = dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Start felodipine is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient with suspected Prinzmetal’s (variant) angina. This condition is caused by transient coronary artery vasospasm, often in the absence of fixed atherosclerotic disease, as confirmed by this patient’s normal coronary angiogram. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as felodipine, amlodipine, or nifedipine, are recommended as first-line agents in UK practice because they directly relax vascular smooth muscle, preventing and relieving vasospasm. They are effective in reducing the frequency and severity of anginal episodes and are usually given as long-acting preparations. NICE guidance for angina and European Society of Cardiology recommendations for vasospastic angina both support the use of calcium channel blockers as initial therapy, with long-acting nitrates reserved as add-on treatment if symptoms persist.

Nicorandil
Start nicorandil is not the most appropriate first-line choice here. Nicorandil has both nitrate-like and potassium channel-opening effects, and can be used for angina, but it is generally reserved for patients whose symptoms are not controlled with first-line agents or who cannot tolerate them. It is not the drug of choice for initial management of vasospastic angina.

Atenolol
Start atenolol is contraindicated in Prinzmetal’s angina. Beta-blockers, particularly non-selective ones, can exacerbate coronary vasospasm by causing unopposed alpha-adrenergic-mediated vasoconstriction. Even cardioselective agents like atenolol are avoided in this condition.

Fluoxetine
Start fluoxetine is not relevant to this presentation. Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used to treat depression and certain anxiety disorders. It has no role in the treatment of angina or coronary vasospasm.

Isosorbide mononitrate
Start isosorbide mononitrate is a reasonable option for vasospastic angina but is usually used as an adjunct to calcium channel blockers rather than as initial monotherapy. Long-acting nitrates reduce preload and dilate coronary vessels, helping to prevent spasm, but tolerance can develop with continuous use, so they are often introduced later in the treatment pathway if CCB monotherapy is insufficient.

stem: A 36-year-old man has presented to the emergency department with palpitations. His heart rate was 138 beats per minute and an ECG showed a likely supraventricular tachycardia. The registrar asks you to draw up 6mg of adenosine. Which of the following drugs may reduce the action of adenosine?
explanation:
Aminophylline
Aminophylline reduces the effect of adenosine. The answer is aminophylline.

Dipyridamole
Dipyridamole classically enhances the action of adenosine. This is commonly remembered with the mnemonic DEAR.

Bupivacaine
Bupivacaine (and other -caines) all also enhance the action of adenosine.

stem: A 46-year-old man presents to the emergency department with palpitations. On examination, he is clinically stable with no signs of shock or cardiac failure. An ECG demonstrates fast atrial fibrillation (AF) which is resolved with IV fluids alone. On review of his medical records, he has had previous episodes of AF but had not been initiated on treatment. A plan is made to commence a sodium channel blocker for rhythm control. He is also advised to start on anticoagulation. What medication has he been commenced on to prevent AF?
explanation:
Flecainide
Flecainide blocks the Nav1.5 sodium channels in the heart. This patient has presented with atrial fibrillation (AF) which appears to be paroxysmal in nature given it resolved without significant intervention and he has had previous episodes in the past. There are several different classes of antiarrhythmic agents that can be used to prevent paroxysmal AF. Class I agents are sodium channel blockers and include flecainide which can be used either continuously (i.e. taken every day) or as required (i.e. when a patient experiences symptoms and therefore are likely experiencing an AF episode) a method known as 'pill in the pocket'.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone can be used to manage refractory AF but is generally reserved for acute management only. Long-term use of amiodarone is associated with significant side effects including interstitial lung disease, thyroid and liver issues. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent and its mechanism of action is via potassium channel blockage.

Digoxin
Digoxin was one of the first antiarrhythmic agents used for AF. With the development of new medications with fewer side effects, it is generally reserved now for patients with concurrent cardiac failure having demonstrated favourable results in these patients. Digoxin's main mechanism of action is via inhibition of the sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase channels.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem can be used for several cardiac issues including arrhythmias when it is classified as a class IV, calcium channel blocker. Diltiazem is typically considered a rate-controlling medication and can also be used to manage conditions such as hypertension and cardiac failure.

Nicorandil
Nicorandil is an anti-anginal agent with both nitrate and potassium channel agonist properties. It is not used in the management of AF.

stem: You are reviewing a 75-year-old male patient with hypertension. He takes 10mg once a day of ramipril and 10mg once a day of amlodipine. His blood pressure remains uncontrolled and you want to start a third agent. His K+ is 4.3 mmol/l. According to the NICE guidelines, what would be the most appropriate third-line agent for this man?
explanation:
Indapamide
This patient is >55 years old and is already on an ACE-inhibitor (ramipril) at the maximum dose and a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) at the maximum dose. According to the NICE guidelines, thiazide-like diuretics are the next line therapy, e.g., chlortalidone (12.5-25.0 mg once daily) or indapamide (1.5 mg modified-release once daily or 2.5 mg once daily). Therefore, the correct answer here is indapamide.

Bendroflumethiazide
NICE state that a thiazide-like diuretic should be used in preference to a conventional thiazide diuretic such as bendroflumethiazide or hydrochlorothiazide. Therefore, these two answers are wrong.

Candesartan
Candesartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) and should not be used in conjunction with an ACE-inhibitor.

Hydrochlorothiazide
NICE state that a thiazide-like diuretic should be used in preference to a conventional thiazide diuretic such as bendroflumethiazide or hydrochlorothiazide. Therefore, these two answers are wrong.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone is used as a fourth agent in resistant hypertension if the K+ is <4.5 mmol/l.

stem: A 74-year-old man with chronic heart failure is reviewed in clinic. His symptoms are controlled with ramipril, bisoprolol, and furosemide but he experiences persistent hypokalaemia. He cannot tolerate potassium supplements due to gastrointestinal side effects. Spironolactone was also trialled but discontinued due to gynaecomastia. To conserve potassium, he is started on amiloride. Which option is the site of action of this drug?
options: Epithelial Na+ channels in the distal convoluted tubule
Na+-Cl- symporters in the distal convoluted tubule
Na+-K+-Cl- cotransporters in the ascending limb
Specific receptors in the cortical collecting ducts
explanation:
Epithelial Na+ channels in the distal convoluted tubule
Amiloride selectively blocks the epithelial sodium transport channels. Epithelial Na+ channels in the distal convoluted tubule is correct. This patient’s hypokalaemia is caused by furosemide, a loop diuretic that increases potassium excretion. Amiloride conserves potassium by blocking epithelial sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts, reducing sodium reabsorption and subsequent potassium secretion.

Aquaporins in the collecting ducts
Aquaporins in the collecting ducts is incorrect. No drugs directly block aquaporins, though tolvaptan indirectly affects them by inhibiting ADH. Blocking aquaporins would increase free water excretion, which could worsen hypovolaemia in a patient already on diuretics. Due to amiloride's relatively weak diuretic effect, it is more appropriate here as an adjunct. Tolvaptan is only licensed for use in polycystic kidney disease and syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion under specialist supervision.

Na+-Cl- symporters in the distal convoluted tubule
Na+-Cl- symporters in the distal convoluted tubule is incorrect as this describes the mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics, like bendroflumethiazide. Thiazides would be harmful, as they increase potassium excretion similarly to furosemide.

Na+-K+-Cl- cotransporters in the ascending limb
Na+-K+-Cl- cotransporters in the ascending limb is incorrect. This describes the mechanism of action of loop diuretics like furosemide, the cause of this patient’s hypokalaemia. Discontinuing this patient's furosemide may worsen their heart failure, as less water excretion causes pulmonary congestion, peripheral oedema, and increased dyspnoea.

Specific receptors in the cortical collecting ducts
Specific receptors in the cortical collecting ducts is incorrect. This describes the target of aldosterone antagonists, such as spironolactone. While they are potassium-sparing, the patient discontinued spironolactone due to gynaecomastia. While eplerenone is less commonly linked with this, this patient is being started on amiloride. If amiloride is ineffective or not tolerated, then this could be considered.

stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department. He was found collapsed by neighbours. An ECG on arrival shows torsades de pointes. Which one of his medications is most likely to have contributed to this presentation?
explanation:
Risperidone
The correct answer is Risperidone. Risperidone, an atypical antipsychotic, is known to cause QT interval prolongation on ECG and can lead to torsades de pointes, a type of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. This condition can be life-threatening and presents with symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, or syncope. In some cases like the one presented in the question, it may lead to sudden collapse due to arrhythmia-induced reduced cardiac output.

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker primarily used for managing hypertension and heart failure. It does not typically cause QT interval prolongation. Instead, it may slow down the heart rate and could potentially exacerbate bradycardia or heart block.

Cimetidine
Cimetidine, which is an H2 receptor antagonist used for treating conditions like peptic ulcer disease and gastroesophageal reflux disease. While cimetidine has been associated with various side effects including gynecomastia and mental status changes in elderly patients, it does not usually cause QT prolongation or torsades de pointes.

Phenytoin
Phenytoin is an antiepileptic drug, can indeed cause cardiovascular side effects but these are generally limited to bradycardia and hypotension when administered intravenously at high doses or rates. It's not typically associated with QT interval prolongation or torsades de pointes.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic commonly used for various infections such as pneumonia and sexually transmitted diseases. While it can have many potential side effects including photosensitivity and gastrointestinal upset, it does not typically affect cardiac conduction or induce QT interval prolongation.

stem: A 67-year-old diabetic gentleman who recently underwent aortic valve replacement presented with a fever, raised inflammatory markers and deranged renal function. Which one of the following organisms contribute to the highest rate of mortality in patients with his condition?
explanation:
Staphylococci
Staphylococci is the leading organism contributing to mortality in infective endocarditis. Staph aureus followed by coagulase-negative staphylococci are two of the most common organisms causing infective endocarditis.

Enterococci
Enterococci - Belongs to the bowel organisms group and contributes to only 15% of mortality.

Streptococci
Streptococci - Only contribute to around 5% of mortality.

Pseudomonas
Pseudomonas - Rare cause of endocarditis, occurs when infected water enters the bloodstream.

HACEK Organisms
HACEK Organisms - Lives on dental gums and are more common in intravenous drug users.

stem: A 56-year-old man attends his GP surgery for a routine blood pressure check and examination. He has no immediate concerns and his past medical history includes hypertension and asthma. He feels well in himself. On examination, he appears well and observations are normal except for a raised blood pressure of 155/87 mmHg. Upon auscultation of the heart, the GP notices an S4 heart sound. The GP then requests an ECG recording. Which part of the ECG does this sound coincide with?
explanation:
P wave
S4 coincides with the P wave on ECG. The correct answer is the P wave. The S4 heart sound is caused by atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle, occurring just before the S1 sound. It may be heard in aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or hypertension. As such, it coincides with the P wave, which represents atrial depolarisation.

QRS complex
The QRS complex is incorrect. This represents ventricular depolarisation, whereas the S4 heart sound is due to atrial contraction.

ST segment
The ST segment is incorrect. This is simply the interval between ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation - it is not associated with a heart sound.

T wave
T waves are an indication of ventricular repolarisation - as such, the S4 heart sound is not linked to these.

U wave
U waves may not always be seen - these are small deflections following T waves. There are a number of theories regarding their origin, including delayed repolarisation of Purkinje fibres. These do not correlate with the S4 sound.

stem: A 64-year-old man attends his GP for an annual health check. He was found to be hypertensive and his GP started ramipril 2.5mg OD. His other medications include lansoprazole 30mg OD, furosemide 20mg OD and atorvastatin 40mg ON. His U+E have generally been stable and a blood test showed: Na+ 139 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 7.5 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 140 µmol/L (55 - 120) eGFR 47 ml/min/1.73m2 One month later the GP requests repeat U+Es: Na+ 139 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 5.6 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 8.5 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 150 µmol/L (55 - 120) eGFR 43 ml/min/1.73m2 An ECG is normal. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management plan, in addition to re-checking the U+E's?
options: Stop ramipril and restart at a lower dose
Advise on a low potassium diet
explanation:
Swap ramipril for another anti-hypertensive
A potassium above 6mmol/L should prompt cessation of ACE inhibitors in a patient with CKD (once other agents that promote hyperkalemia have been stopped) NICE Clinical Guideline 182 - in patients with CKD, potassium above 6mmol/L should prompt cessation of ACE inhibitors in a patient with CKD (once other agents that promote hyperkalemia have been stopped). In this case, there is no other medicine that can be stopped first in an attempt to bring down the potassium. All the other options would decrease serum potassium, but would not conform to the NICE guidelines in this situation.

Stop ramipril and restart at a lower dose
Stop ramipril and restart at a lower dose is not the most appropriate management plan according to NICE guidelines, as potassium is not above 6mmol/L.

Increase dose of furosemide
Increase dose of furosemide would decrease serum potassium, but would not conform to the NICE guidelines in this situation.

Advise on a low potassium diet
Advise on a low potassium diet would decrease serum potassium, but would not conform to the NICE guidelines in this situation.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute swelling of his face, lips, and tongue. He has no pruritus or rash. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension, and he has no known allergies. His pulse is 70 bpm, blood pressure is 135/95 mmHg, oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air, and respiratory rate is 14 /min. Auscultation of the chest reveals equal air entry bilaterally, with no added sounds and no observable rash. Which option is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Lisinopril
Lisinopril is correct. This patient’s acute facial, lip, and tongue swelling without pruritus or rash is characteristic of angioedema without urticaria, most commonly caused by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors like lisinopril. ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin levels by preventing its breakdown, leading to increased vascular permeability and tissue swelling, particularly in the face, lips, and tongue. The absence of wheezing, hypotension, or skin rash makes an allergic reaction less likely. ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema can occur at any time, even after years of use, requiring immediate discontinuation of the drug to prevent recurrence.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect as calcium channel blockers like amlodipine are not known to cause angioedema affecting the face and airways. Amlodipine instead works by inhibiting calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle, leading to vasodilation. This can cause peripheral oedema which is thought to be due to arteriolar dilation, increasing capillary pressure, leading to fluid extravasation. However, this tends to affect the feet and legs rather than the face.

Atorvastatin
Atorvastatin is incorrect. Angioedema is not commonly associated with atorvastatin, and its incidence is significantly low compared to ACE inhibitors, as it does not share the same mechanisms leading to bradykinin accumulation. Instead, it can cause myopathy or rhabdomyolysis, presenting with muscle pain, weakness, and elevated creatine kinase rather than the angioedema seen in this patient.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect as thiazide diuretics like bendroflumethiazide are not known to cause angioedema affecting the face. Bendroflumethiazide works by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, leading to increased urine output and decreased blood volume. This would be more likely to cause dehydration rather than the accumulation of fluid. It is also more likely to cause electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalaemia, which can lead to muscle weakness, palpitations, or arrhythmias, which are not seen here.

Candesartan
Candesartan is incorrect. Candesartan, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), can rarely cause angioedema, but this is much less common than with ACE inhibitors. ARBs minimally affect bradykinin compared to ACE inhibitors, but rare angioedema can still occur via alternative pathways. Since patients who develop ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema may still be at risk with ARBs, caution is required when switching medications.

stem: A neonate female born at 37 weeks gestation develops severe cyanosis 1 hour after birth. She develops worsening respiratory distress and becomes highly tachypnoeic with difficulty feeding. She is soon transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit for supportive treatment. Her mother did not seek any antenatal care and the baby was born via an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery. On physical examination, the neonate is cyanosed and lethargic. Her vital signs were as follows: respiratory rate 62/min, oxygen saturation 84% (on 60% oxygen), heart rate 160/min, blood pressure 96/66 mmHg. Cardiac auscultation reveals a loud S2 heart sound. Chest x-ray shows the cardiac silhouette with an 'eggs on a string' appearance. Electrocardiogram (ECG) shows a right ventricular dominance. Further diagnostic workup with echocardiography confirms a congenital heart defect. Which of the following is the most likely underlying embryological pathology in this neonate's congenital heart defect?
options: Absent tricuspid valve and hypoplastic right ventricle
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
Aortic narrowing near insertion of ductus arteriosus
explanation:
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
Transposition of great vessels is due to the failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral. The clinical stem here is significant for a cyanotic heart disease. The clinical findings as well as the classic X-ray description point towards a diagnosis of transposition of great vessels which is caused by the failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral during early life.

Absent tricuspid valve and hypoplastic right ventricle
Absent tricuspid valve and hypoplastic right ventricle are seen in tricuspid atresia (cyanotic heart defect).

Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum is seen in Tetralogy of Fallot (cyanotic heart defect). The x-ray in this condition would show a 'boot-shaped' heart.

Defect in interatrial septum
A defect in the interatrial septum is present in the atrial septal defect (non-cyanotic).

Aortic narrowing near insertion of ductus arteriosus
Aortic narrowing near the insertion of ductus arteriosus occurs in aortic coarctation.

stem: What is the main reason for checking the urea and electrolytes prior to commencing a patient on amiodarone?
explanation:
To detect hypokalaemia
All antiarrhythmic drugs have the potential to cause arrhythmias. Coexistent hypokalaemia significantly increases this risk.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with palpitations. Her ECG shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 180 bpm. She is haemodynamically stable. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre is performed, which successfully terminates the arrhythmia. Which physiological mechanism is primarily responsible for the termination of her supraventricular tachycardia?
options: Reduced cardiac preload during the strain phase
Sympathetic activation in response to reduced blood pressure
Initial transient increase in aortic pressure at the onset of strain
Baroreflex-mediated vagal stimulation after release of strain
Sudden decrease in intrathoracic pressure on release of strain
explanation:
Baroreflex-mediated vagal stimulation after release of strain
Baroreflex-mediated vagal stimulation after release of strain is the correct answer. The therapeutic effect of the Valsalva manoeuvre occurs in Phase IV, the 'overshoot' phase. After the patient stops straining, the intrathoracic pressure normalises, allowing a sudden surge of venous return to the heart. This bolus of blood is ejected by the heart into a peripheral circulation that remains vasoconstricted from the sympathetic response during the strain phase (Phase II). The combination of increased cardiac output and high systemic vascular resistance causes a transient overshoot in arterial blood pressure. This sharp rise is detected by baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, triggering a powerful reflex increase in parasympathetic (vagal) tone. This vagal discharge slows conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node, which is sufficient to interrupt the re-entrant circuit responsible for most common forms of SVT, such as atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT), thus terminating the arrhythmia.

Reduced cardiac preload during the strain phase
Reduced cardiac preload during the strain phase is incorrect. This describes the central event of Phase II of the manoeuvre. The sustained high intrathoracic pressure compresses the great veins, impeding venous return to the right atrium and thereby reducing cardiac preload. This leads to a fall in stroke volume and blood pressure. However, this physiological change itself does not terminate the tachycardia. In fact, the body's response to this drop in blood pressure is to increase sympathetic tone and heart rate, which is counterproductive to terminating an SVT.

Sympathetic activation in response to reduced blood pressure
Sympathetic activation in response to reduced blood pressure is incorrect. This physiological response also occurs during Phase II. The fall in blood pressure, caused by the reduced preload, is detected by baroreceptors. This triggers a compensatory reflex increase in sympathetic nervous system activity, leading to peripheral vasoconstriction and an increase in heart rate. This sympathetic surge helps to restore blood pressure towards normal during the strain but would tend to perpetuate, rather than terminate, a tachycardia. The therapeutic effect comes from the subsequent rebound parasympathetic activity.

Initial transient increase in aortic pressure at the onset of strain
Initial transient increase in aortic pressure at the onset of strain is incorrect. This describes Phase I of the Valsalva manoeuvre. When the patient first begins to strain, the increase in intrathoracic pressure mechanically compresses the aorta and large arteries, forcing blood out into the periphery. This causes a very brief, transient spike in blood pressure. This phase is too short and the mechanism is not powerful enough to generate the significant vagal tone required to terminate an established SVT. The key events occur later in the sequence.

Sudden decrease in intrathoracic pressure on release of strain
Sudden decrease in intrathoracic pressure on release of strain is incorrect. This describes Phase III of the manoeuvre. While this event is the critical trigger for the final therapeutic phase, it is not the terminating mechanism itself. The sudden drop in intrathoracic pressure causes a brief, further dip in systemic arterial pressure as blood pools transiently in the pulmonary circulation. The key therapeutic event is the physiological consequence of this pressure release, which is the subsequent surge in venous return and the resultant blood pressure overshoot in Phase IV.

stem: A 10-day-old neonate born prematurely at 34 weeks' gestation has been slow to wean off the ventilator since birth. On examination, she has been found to have a continuous heart murmur. An echocardiogram has detected a patent ductus arteriosus. No other structural heart abnormalities have been found. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and mildly congested lung fields. What initial treatment should be started to manage this condition?
explanation:
Indomethacin
Preterm infants with haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus 1 week after birth - give ibuprofen/indomethacin to promote duct closure. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as indomethacin and ibuprofen) inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, therefore accelerating the closure of the DA and is an effective non-surgical treatment.

Emergency surgery
Surgery is generally only performed if non-surgical measures have been unsuccessful.

Beta-blockers
There is no role for using beta-blockers in this condition.

Intravenous fluids
Intravenous fluids are of no benefit in treating this condition and may worsen heart failure.

Prostaglandins
Prostaglandins would have the opposite effect i.e. maintaining the patency of the DA. They are sometimes used where a PDA is desirable, such as if there is co-existing right-to-left shunt defect where the PDA may be the only way for oxygenated blood to mix with deoxygenated blood.

stem: A 75-year-old female presents diaphoretic and distressed with new onset sternal chest pain radiating through to the back. She has a past history of hypertension on lercanidipine. On examination her blood pressure is 190/70 mmHg and there is an early diastolic murmur heard best at the left sternal edge. Her ECG is unremarkable. What is the next best course of action?
explanation:
CT angiogram with contrast
This is a classic example of an aortic dissection causing aortic regurgitation. The best investigation is going to be a CT angiogram with IV contrast because the IV contrast will be able to best demonstrate the size and extent of the false lumen. The chest X-ray may show a widened mediastinum, but unfortunately it is not a sensitive or specific investigation as 20% of patients present with normal chest X-ray and there are many causes of a widened mediastinum. However, the chest X-ray is a useful first line investigation for this condition because of how readily available it is, and useful for ruling out many other conditions. Looking for a separation of the intimal calcification from the outer aortic soft tissue border by 10 mm is an indication of the presence of a dissection. The CT angiogram with contrast will provide the most amount of information by far, and can demonstrate the extent of the dissection.

Aspirin/clopidogrel/IV heparin
Aspirin/clopidogrel/IV heparin is not the next best course of action in this scenario. While these medications are used in the management of acute coronary syndromes, they are not the primary investigation for a suspected aortic dissection.

Cardiac catheterisation
Cardiac catheterisation is not the next best course of action. While it can be useful in certain cardiovascular emergencies, it is not the primary investigation for a suspected aortic dissection.

Urgent echocardiogram
An urgent echocardiogram is a reasonable investigation, but it will not demonstrate the extent of the vessel lesion as well as a CT angiogram with contrast. The CT angiogram will provide more detailed information about the extent of the dissection.

stem: A 69-year-old man who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation asks for advice. He is due to have a tooth extraction at the dentist and is unsure what to do with regards to his 'blood-thinning' tablets. There is no other past medical history of note. The last INR was taken two weeks ago and reported as 2.8 with his target INR being 2.0-3.0. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Admit to hospital + switch to subcutaneous low-molecular weight heparin prior to extraction
Switch to aspirin prior to extraction
Check INR 72 hours before procedure, proceed if INR < 4.0
Check INR 72 hours before procedure, proceed if INR < 2.5
Admit to hospital + switch to intravenous heparin prior to extraction
explanation:
Check INR 72 hours before procedure, proceed if INR < 4.0
Dentistry in warfarinised patients - check INR 72 hours before procedure, proceed if INR < 4.0 The BNF gives specific advice with regards to this, in the section 'Prescribing in dental practice'. If a patient has a history of an unstable INR then it should be checked within 24 hours of the dental procedure.

stem: A 74-year-old man attends the clinic with gum swelling. He has a past medical history of hypertension and angina. His regular medications include amlodipine, aspirin, isosorbide mononitrate, and ramipril. Blood results are as follows: Hb 145 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 152 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 135 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 4.8 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 56 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 2 mg/L (< 5) What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Amlodipine
Amlodipine may cause gingival hyperplasia. Amlodipine-induced gingival overgrowth (AIGO) is characterised by an increase in the volume of connective tissue matrix in the gingiva. It is a relatively common side effect of treatment with calcium channel blockers.

Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is incorrect. Although AML is associated with gingival hyperplasia, it is a very rare condition and there is no evidence of it based on the patient's full blood count.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin is not associated with gingival hyperplasia.

Isosorbide mononitrate
Isosorbide mononitrate is incorrect. Isosorbide mononitrate is not associated with gingival hyperplasia.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Ramipril is not associated with gingival hyperplasia.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of fevers, night sweats and lethargy. On examination, you note several Janeway lesions on his hands. There is a collapsing pulse and you note an early diastolic murmur. You take multiple sets of blood cultures and commence the patient on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed infective endocarditis. A trans-thoracic echo identifies large vegetation on the aortic valve with associated aortic regurgitation. You note the patient has a background of metastatic colorectal cancer and is currently receiving palliative chemotherapy. In light of the patient's past medical history, which of the following organisms are most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Streptococcus gallolyticus
Streptococcus gallolyticus is the subtype of Streptococcus bovis most linked with colorectal cancer. It is strongly linked with colorectal cancer, and is a key cause of infective endocarditis in elderly and immunocompromised patients.

Brucella
Brucellosis is the most common bacterial disease contracted from contact with animals - most commonly sheep and goats. Infection can be acquired from consumption of unprocessed animal products in endemic countries of the Mediterranean and middle East such as Syria, Iraq, Turkey, Greece and Tunisia. Infection is characterised by a malodorous 'wet-hay smell.'

Coxiella burnetii
Coxiella burnetti is a culture-negative cause of infective endocarditis. The source of infection is typically an abattoir, cattle/sheep or it may be inhaled from infected dust.

Staphylococcus epidermidis
Coagulase-negative Staphylococci such as Staphylococcus epidermidis commonly colonise indwelling lines and are the most common cause of endocarditis in patients following prosthetic valve surgery.

Streptococcus viridans
Streptococcus viridans accounts for around 20% of infective endocarditis. The two most notable viridans streptococci are Streptococcus mitis and Streptococcus sanguinis. They are both commonly found in the mouth and in particular dental plaque, so endocarditis caused by these organisms is linked with poor dental hygiene or following a dental procedure.

stem: A 59-year-old man of Indian origin is seen in clinic for a hypertension review. He shows you a diary of blood pressure recordings he has taken at home, with measurements consistently above 150/90 mmHg. He takes amlodipine and atorvastatin; he has been established on this regime for one year and doses have been optimised. What would be the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue to monitor blood pressure at home and review in one month
Stop amlodipine and trial ramipril instead
Stop amlodipine and trial ramipril with indapamide instead
explanation:
Add indapamide
The correct answer is to commence indapamide in addition to amlodipine. This patient has stage 2 hypertension on home-monitoring, with other cardiovascular risk factors noted, established on a calcium channel blocker. As per the NICE treatment algorithm, the next step would be to add an ACE inhibitor (ACEi), angiotensin-receptor-blocker (ARB) or a thiazide-like diuretic. Accordingly, the correct answer is indapamide which is a thiazide-like diuretic.

Add bendroflumethiazide
Adding bendroflumethiazide in addition to amlodipine is incorrect. Bendroflumethiazide is a thiazide diuretic and an easy point of confusion. Only thiazide-like diuretics, such as indapamide, are recommended in the next step of the algorithm.

Continue to monitor blood pressure at home and review in one month
Continuing blood pressure monitoring at home and reviewing in one month would not be appropriate. The patient has already been monitoring blood pressure at home, and with the evidence of persisting hypertension in addition to other cardiovascular risk factors, treatment of his hypertension should be escalated.

Stop amlodipine and trial ramipril instead
Stopping amlodipine and trialling ramipril instead is incorrect. Ramipril could be added in addition to amlodipine but not in replacement of it. Combination therapy is the recommendation as per the treatment algorithm.

Stop amlodipine and trial ramipril with indapamide instead
Stopping amlodipine and trialling ramipril with indapamide instead is incorrect. An ACEi such as ramipril or a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide can be added in addition to a calcium channel blocker, but the combination should not be commenced in replacement of amlodipine.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and orthopnoea. He has a past medical history of ischaemic heart disease. His medications include aspirin, bisoprolol, ramipril and spironolactone. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. Observations: Heart rate 99 beats per minute Respiratory rate 24/minute Oxygen saturations 92% on room air Blood pressure 154/88 mmHg Temperature 37C Chest auscultation reveals bilateral crackles extending to the midzones. There are no murmurs. There is no peripheral oedema. Based on the likely diagnosis, which of the following is an early sign of this condition?
explanation:
S3
Gallop rhythm (S3) is an early sign of LVF. The patient presents with shortness of breath and orthopnoea in association with bilateral crackles extending to the midzone with evidence of respiratory failure. On a background of ischaemic heart disease, this is likely caused by left ventricular failure. An S3 gallop rhythm is an early sign of left ventricular failure.

Soft S1
Soft S1 is incorrect. This is caused by a prolonged PR, severe mitral stenosis or mitral regurgitation. We are told there are no murmurs.

Absent S2
Absent S2 is incorrect. This is a sign of severe aortic stenosis. However, this sign will be present irrespective of whether or not this patient has developed heart failure signs and symptoms.

Loud P2
Loud P2 is incorrect. This is an early sign of pulmonary hypertension, which may cause right-sided heart failure. However, bilateral crackles on auscultation suggest left-sided heart failure on a background of ischaemic heart disease.

S4
S4 is incorrect. This is an extra sound caused by atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle. It is associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and hypertension but not acute LVF.

stem: An 88-year-old woman presents with palpitations for three days. Her medical history includes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), symptomatic postural hypotension, wheelchair-bound, and recurrent falls. Her ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate of 126 bpm. A decision to rate control is decided. With the risk of worsening postural hypotension with other rate-control agents, she is given an oral rate-control medication that does not induce hypotension and is a weakly positive inotrope. What is the mechanism of action of this rate-controlling medication?
explanation:
Inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump
Digoxin - inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump. Digoxin would be an appropriate medication in this scenario given its lack of effect on blood pressure, and the patient's history of HFrEF and her immobility. Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump causing increased intracellular sodium and calcium levels leading to a decrease in conduction through the AV node.

Blocks the voltage-gated sodium channels
Class I antiarrhythmics, such as lidocaine, work by blocking the voltage-gated sodium channels in phase 0 of the cardiac action potential. Class I antiarrhythmics such as flecainide are used for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation. Flecainide is contraindicated in this woman as she has heart failure. These class I antiarrhythmics are not used in rate control management of atrial fibrillation.

Inhibiting the Na+/Cl- symporter
Thiazide diuretics decrease intravascular volume by inhibiting the Na+/Cl- symporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Thiazide diuretics would not be first-line diuretics if this woman is clinically overloaded. Side effects of thiazides include hypercalcemia, hypokalaemia, and hyperglycaemia.

Inhibits the Na+/K+/Cl2- cotransporter
Loop diuretics, such as furosemide, inhibit the Na+/K+/Cl2cotransporter in the thick ascending loop of Henle. The woman has presented with palpitations and no overt signs of heart failure so furosemide will not be beneficial in this scenario. Side effects of loop diuretics include hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia, and hyperglycaemia.

Muscarinic receptor antagonist
Muscarinic receptor antagonism medications are not used to treat tachyarrhythmias. Atropine's mechanism of action to increase the heart rate is through cardiac muscarinic receptor antagonism. Atropine is a first-line treatment for hemodynamically unstable bradycardia. Its use is limited in hemodynamically unstable bradycardia caused by infra-nodal heart blocks.

stem: A 62-year-old man who had a mechanical mitral valve replacement four years ago is reviewed. What long term antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?
options: Aspirin + clopidogrel for the first 12 months
explanation:
Warfarin
Prosthetic heart valves - antithrombotic therapy: bioprosthetic: aspirin mechanical: warfarin + aspirin Following the 2017 European Society of Cardiology guidelines, aspirin is only normally given in addition if there is an additional indication, e.g. ischaemic heart disease. Direct acting oral anticoagulants are not used in patients with a mechanical heart valve.

Nothing
Prosthetic heart valves - antithrombotic therapy: bioprosthetic: aspirin mechanical: warfarin + aspirin

Direct acting oral anticoagulants
Direct acting oral anticoagulants are not used in patients with a mechanical heart valve.

Aspirin
Following the 2017 European Society of Cardiology guidelines, aspirin is only normally given in addition if there is an additional indication, e.g. ischaemic heart disease.

stem: A 78-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia is treated with clarithromycin. Two days later, she has a witnessed syncopal episode. She is now alert. Her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg and her heart rate is 110 bpm. An urgent ECG shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that appear to twist around the isoelectric baseline. The rhythm is intermittent. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
explanation:
IV magnesium sulfate
IV magnesium sulfate is used to treat torsades de pointes. The clinical presentation and ECG findings are characteristic of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), a specific form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with a prolonged QT interval. The patient has a clear risk factor, which is the recent initiation of clarithromycin, a macrolide antibiotic known to prolong the QT interval. The management of TdP differs significantly from other forms of ventricular tachycardia. IV magnesium sulfate is the first-line and most appropriate immediate treatment for Torsades de Pointes, regardless of the patient's baseline serum magnesium level. Magnesium is thought to stabilise the cardiac membrane and block the influx of calcium, thereby terminating the arrhythmia. It is effective in both preventing recurrent episodes and terminating ongoing ones.

DC cardioversion
DC cardioversion is reserved for patients with TdP who are haemodynamically unstable due to a sustained arrhythmia or who degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. In this scenario, the patient had a syncopal episode but is now conscious, and the rhythm is described as intermittent. Therefore, immediate synchronised cardioversion is not the first-line approach; medical therapy with magnesium should be administered first.

IV adrenaline
IV adrenaline is a key component of the cardiac arrest algorithm for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. This patient has a pulse and is conscious, so adrenaline is not indicated. Its administration could increase myocardial irritability and potentially provoke further arrhythmias.

IV amiodarone
IV amiodarone is a common treatment for many ventricular arrhythmias, but it must be used with extreme caution or avoided entirely in patients with TdP. Amiodarone itself can prolong the QT interval, and administering it could potentially worsen the arrhythmia or make it more frequent. Other antiarrhythmics that prolong the QT interval, such as sotalol and Class Ia agents, are also contraindicated.

Temporary cardiac pacing
Temporary cardiac pacing, specifically overdrive pacing at a rate of 90-110 bpm, is a highly effective second-line treatment for TdP, particularly if it is recurrent or refractory to magnesium therapy. Increasing the heart rate shortens the QT interval, which suppresses the early afterdepolarisations that trigger TdP. However, it is an invasive procedure that is not the most appropriate immediate step compared to the rapid administration of intravenous magnesium.

stem: A 58-year-old man with no past medical history of note is admitted to hospital with crushing central chest pain. ECG on arrival shows anterior ST elevation and he is subsequently thrombolysed with a good resolution of symptoms and ECG changes. Four weeks following the event, which combination of drugs should he be taking?
options: ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + ticagrelor
explanation:
ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + ticagrelor
The correct answer is ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + ticagrelor. Following an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), current guidelines recommend dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (preferably ticagrelor) for 12 months. Additionally, patients should receive an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and high-intensity statin for secondary prevention.

ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin
ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin is incorrect as it only includes single antiplatelet therapy. Following STEMI, DAPT is essential to prevent stent thrombosis and reduce recurrent cardiovascular events.

Spironolactone + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin
Spironolactone + beta-blocker + statin + aspirin is incorrect. While spironolactone has a role in heart failure management, it is not routinely indicated post-MI unless there is significant left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤40%) or heart failure.

ACE inhibitor + statin + aspirin + clopidogrel
ACE inhibitor + statin + aspirin + clopidogrel is incorrect as it omits a beta-blocker, which is essential post-MI to reduce mortality and prevent arrhythmias. While clopidogrel is an acceptable P2Y12 inhibitor, ticagrelor is preferred due to superior outcomes.

Beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + clopidogrel
Beta-blocker + statin + aspirin + clopidogrel is incorrect as it omits an ACE inhibitor, which is important for reducing adverse cardiac remodelling post-MI and improving long-term outcomes.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the office due to exertional dyspnea that has progressed over the last year. She can hardly walk a block without stopping to rest. On physical examination, the patient has a loud second heart sound over the left upper sternal border, increased jugular venous pressure, and a palpable right ventricular impulse. Chest x-ray shows clear lungs. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
explanation:
Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension is a cause of a loud S2 (due to a loud P2). Pulmonary hypertension commonly presents with progressive dyspnea, and patients may also experience exertional angina or syncope. Physical examination reveals a loud pulmonic component (P2) of S2, caused by forceful pulmonic valve closure in the setting of high pulmonary arterial pressure.

Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is common in elderly and presents with a systolic murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border. It presents with a soft S2, not a loud S2.

Hypertensive heart disease
Hypertensive heart disease causes left ventricular hypertrophy, leading to impaired ventricular compliance and diastolic heart failure.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard at the left sternal border.

Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block can delay the closure of the aortic valve, leading to a later occurrence of the aortic component (A2) of S2 and narrowed or paradoxical splitting.

stem: Which one of the following types of hyperlipidaemia are eruptive xanthoma most commonly associated with?
explanation:
Familial hypertriglyceridaemia
The correct answer is Familial hypertriglyceridaemia. Eruptive xanthomas are skin lesions that occur due to the deposition of lipids in the skin. They are most commonly associated with conditions that cause high levels of triglycerides, such as familial hypertriglyceridaemia. In this condition, there is an increase in very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), which is rich in triglycerides. The excess triglycerides deposit in the skin leading to eruptive xanthomas.

Familial hypercholesterolaemia
Familial hypercholesterolaemia is characterised by elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) rather than triglycerides. It typically leads to tendon xanthomas, not eruptive xanthomas which are more related to high levels of triglycerides.

Familial combined hyperlipidaemia
Familial combined hyperlipidaemia involves an elevation of both cholesterol and triglyceride levels but eruptive xanthomas are less common compared with familial hypertriglyceridaemia because the level of triglycerides does not reach as high.

Remnant hyperlipidaemia
Remnant hyperlipidaemia, also known as Type III Hyperlipoproteinemia or dysbetalipoproteinemia, is a rare genetic disorder characterized by improper breakdown (metabolism) of certain fatty materials known as lipids, specifically cholesterol and triglycerides. This condition may lead to palmar or tubo-eruptive xanthoma but it's less common compared with familial hypertriglyceridemia.

Hyperlipidaemia secondary to nephrotic syndrome
Hyperlipidaemia secondary to nephrotic syndrome can cause increased cholesterol and/or triglyceride levels due to loss of proteins involved in lipid metabolism through the kidneys. However, while it can cause lipid abnormalities, it doesn't typically result in eruptive xanthomas like familial hypertriglyceridaemia does.

stem: A 78-year-old woman attends a cardiology clinic with persistent exertional dyspnoea. She has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. An echocardiogram last month confirmed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% with grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. She is currently taking furosemide and is clinically euvolaemic. Her latest blood results are: Na+ 140 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 8.1 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 110 µmol/L (55 - 120) eGFR 55 ml/min/1.73m2 (>60) What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
explanation:
Start dapagliflozin
Start dapagliflozin is the correct answer. This patient has symptomatic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), defined by an LVEF >50% and evidence of diastolic dysfunction. Recent UK guidelines recommend a combination of a sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) as first-line therapy to improve outcomes in HFpEF. SGLT2 inhibitors, such as dapagliflozin, have demonstrated a significant reduction in heart failure hospitalisations and cardiovascular mortality in this patient group, irrespective of diabetes status. Given her co-existing type 2 diabetes, this is a particularly beneficial choice.

Start bisoprolol
Start bisoprolol is incorrect. While beta-blockers are a cornerstone of management for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), they are not recommended as routine first-line therapy for HFpEF. Their use is reserved for patients with specific co-morbidities, such as atrial fibrillation requiring rate control or ischaemic heart disease, neither of which is mentioned in the scenario.

Start ramipril
Start ramipril is incorrect. ACE inhibitors, like beta-blockers, are fundamental in HFrEF management. However, large clinical trials have failed to show a consistent prognostic benefit in patients with HFpEF. Therefore, they are not recommended as a first-line treatment specifically for HFpEF, although they may be used to manage comorbidities like hypertension.

Start spironolactone
Start spironolactone is a strong alternative but less ideal as the initial step in this specific case. Spironolactone, an MRA, is also a recommended first-line agent for HFpEF. However, its initiation requires caution in patients with borderline renal function or potassium levels at the higher end of the normal range due to the risk of hyperkalaemia. With an eGFR of 55 ml/min/1.73m² and a potassium of 4.8 mmol/L, starting an SGLT2 inhibitor first may be a safer initial strategy, with the potential to add an MRA later with careful monitoring.

Increase furosemide dose
Increase furosemide dose is incorrect. Loop diuretics are used for symptomatic management of fluid overload. The patient is described as being clinically euvolaemic, so there is no indication to increase the diuretic dose. Doing so would risk dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities without offering any long-term prognostic benefit.

stem: A 34-year-old man is investigated following an unexplained collapse whilst at work. A resting ECG shows convex ST elevation in V1-V3 with a partial right bundle branch block pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Brugada syndrome
The correct answer is Brugada syndrome. This condition is characterised by ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads V1-V3 with a partial or complete right bundle branch block pattern on ECG. It is associated with sudden cardiac death due to ventricular arrhythmias, particularly ventricular fibrillation. The collapse at work could be a manifestation of such an arrhythmia. Brugada syndrome typically presents in healthy adults and can be unmasked by fever, alcohol or certain medications.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) is incorrect because this condition typically presents with exercise or stress-induced bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia without any baseline ECG abnormalities. CPVT does not cause ST elevations on resting ECG.

Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) can also lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death but it is usually associated with a harsh systolic murmur that increases on Valsalva manoeuvre, not ST elevation in V1-V3. On ECG, HOCM often shows left ventricular hypertrophy rather than the specific changes seen in Brugada syndrome.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) might present with similar symptoms as Brugada syndrome, but the characteristic ECG findings are T wave inversions in the right precordial leads and epsilon waves, not ST segment elevation.

Normal variant
While some healthy individuals may exhibit minor non-specific ST and T wave changes on their ECGs, the described pattern of convex ST elevation in V1-V3 with a partial right bundle branch block is too specific to be considered a normal variant.

stem: After sending several invitations, 62-year-old Mr Bentley attends the surgery for his medication review. He has not been into the surgery for nearly two years. He explains he works away during the week so finds it difficult to attend appointments. His medications are allopurinol 200mg, candesartan 8mg, indapamide 2.5mg, omeprazole 20mg and salbutamol inhaler as required. His blood pressure, which you repeat a couple of times, is 166/95mmHg. He says he does remember to take his medications nearly every day, so you suggest starting him on another medication to lower his blood pressure. Which class of antihypertensive medication should be added next, according to NICE?
explanation:
Calcium channel blocker
Calcium channel blocker. Correct, this patient is already on candesartan (an angiotensin II receptor blocker) and indapamide (a thiazide-like diuretic), so the third-line treatment is a calcium channel blocker, such as amlodipine.

Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Incorrect as the patient is already on candesartan - an angiotensin II receptor blocker - which should not be combined with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.

Beta-blocker
Beta-blocker. This is a 4th-line option but this patient is on a salbutamol inhaler, suggesting he may have asthma, so it might be contraindicated.

Loop diuretic
Loop diuretic. Incorrect, loop diuretics (for example furosemide) are not a routine treatment for hypertension.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone. This is a possible 4th-line option, as long as the potassium level is not greater than 4.5mmol/L.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding warfarin is correct?
options: Warfarin can be used when breast-feeding
Hypothyroidism may develop in a small minority of patients
Aortic prosthetic valves generally require a higher INR than mitral valves
The target INR following a pulmonary embolism is 3.5
All patients with an INR of greater than 6.0 should be given vitamin K
explanation:
Warfarin can be used when breast-feeding
The correct answer is 'Warfarin can be used when breast-feeding'. According to the British National Formulary (BNF), warfarin is safe to use during breastfeeding as it is not excreted in breast milk. This means that there is no risk of causing harm to the baby.

Hypothyroidism may develop in a small minority of patients
Hypothyroidism may develop in a small minority of patients: This statement is incorrect. There are no clinical studies or evidence that suggest warfarin causes hypothyroidism. Warfarin acts by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, it has no effect on thyroid function.

Aortic prosthetic valves generally require a higher INR than mitral valves
Aortic prosthetic valves generally require a higher INR than mitral valves: This statement is also incorrect. In fact, the opposite is true. Mitral prosthetic valves generally require a higher INR than aortic ones due to their higher thrombotic risk. The target INR for mitral mechanical prosthetic valves should be 2.5-3.5, whereas for aortic mechanical prosthetic valves, it should be 2.0-3.0 according to NICE guidelines.

The target INR following a pulmonary embolism is 3.5
The target INR following a pulmonary embolism is 3.5: This statement is incorrect as well. According to NICE guidelines, the target INR for the treatment of venous thromboembolism (which includes pulmonary embolism) with warfarin should be 2.5 (with an acceptable range of 2-3).

All patients with an INR of greater than 6.0 should be given vitamin K
All patients with an INR of greater than 6.0 should be given vitamin K: This statement isn't always true because the management depends on whether the patient has bleeding or not and other individual patient factors such as comorbidities and risk of thromboembolism if anticoagulation was reversed temporarily with Vitamin K according to BNF and NICE guidelines.

stem: You review a 24-year-old woman who has recently been diagnosed as having long QT syndrome type I (LQTS1). You are discussing the need to avoid certain drugs and other aggravating factors. Which one of the following should be avoided if possible?
explanation:
Sertraline
The correct answer is Sertraline. Long QT syndrome type I (LQTS1) is a genetic disorder that affects the heart's electrical activity, causing potentially life-threatening arrhythmias. Certain drugs, including some antidepressants such as sertraline, can exacerbate these arrhythmias in patients with LQTS1. Sertraline has been classified as a drug with 'possible risk' of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), a specific type of ventricular tachycardia that can lead to sudden cardiac death, by the Arizona Centre for Education and Research on Therapeutics (AZCERT). Therefore, it should be avoided if possible in patients diagnosed with LQTS1.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is an immunosuppressive drug mainly used in the treatment of cancers and autoimmune diseases. While it may have various side effects, there is no known association between methotrexate and prolongation of the QT interval or increased risk of TdP.

Grapefruit juice
Grapefruit juice can interact with several medications by inhibiting cytochrome P450 enzymes and affecting their metabolism. However, it does not directly affect cardiac ion channels or cause QT prolongation.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant medication used primarily in the treatment of epilepsy and neuropathic pain. It has not been associated with significant QT prolongation or increased risk of TdP.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline, an antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections, also does not have a notable association with QT prolongation or increased risk of TdP.

stem: A 68-year-old man with known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 35%) attends a cardiology follow-up clinic. He is taking ramipril, bisoprolol, spironolactone, and dapagliflozin. Despite this, he remains fatigued with dyspnoea on moderate exertion. His recent blood tests are shown below. Hb 138 g/L (135 - 180) Ferritin 85 ng/mL (30 - 400) Transferrin saturation 18% (20 - 50) Creatinine 110 µmol/L (60 - 120) What is the most appropriate next step in his management?
explanation:
Intravenous iron infusion
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): iron deficiency should be treated with IV iron therapy if Hb < 150 g/L, once other causes of iron-deficiency have been excluded. This patient has symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) despite being on optimal medical therapy. The blood results demonstrate functional iron deficiency, defined in heart failure as a ferritin <100 ng/mL or a transferrin saturation (TSAT) <20%. This patient's ferritin is 85 ng/mL and TSAT is 18%. NICE guidelines recommend treating iron deficiency in patients with HFrEF and a haemoglobin below 150 g/L to improve symptoms, exercise capacity, and quality of life. Intravenous iron is recommended over oral preparations due to better efficacy and absorption in this patient group. His persistent fatigue is very likely attributable to this iron deficiency.

Add ivabradine
Add ivabradine is incorrect. Ivabradine is a second-line therapy for HFrEF, indicated for symptomatic patients who are in sinus rhythm with a heart rate persistently ≥75 bpm, despite an optimised dose of a betablocker. The clinical scenario does not provide any information about the patient's heart rate or rhythm, so there is no clear indication for this medication based on the data given.

Oral iron supplementation
Oral iron supplementation is less appropriate. While it is a standard treatment for iron deficiency in the general population, its absorption is often impaired in patients with heart failure due to factors like gut oedema and systemic inflammation. Clinical trials have consistently shown that intravenous iron is superior to oral iron for replenishing iron stores and improving functional outcomes in patients with HFrEF. Therefore, intravenous administration is the preferred route.

Refer for colonoscopy
Refer for colonoscopy is an important consideration, as iron deficiency in a 68-year-old man warrants investigation for an underlying cause, most commonly gastrointestinal blood loss. However, the question asks for the most appropriate next step in the management of his heart failure symptoms. Treating the iron deficiency with an intravenous infusion will directly address his fatigue and dyspnoea. This treatment can be administered while concurrently arranging investigations into the cause of the deficiency.

Switch ramipril to sacubitril/valsartan
Switch ramipril to sacubitril/valsartan is a key therapeutic step for patients with HFrEF who remain symptomatic despite treatment with an ACE inhibitor. While this is an important consideration for his long-term management, the investigations have revealed a specific, reversible cause for his current symptoms (iron deficiency). Addressing this identified problem is the most appropriate immediate step. The decision to switch to an ARNI can be revisited after his iron status has been corrected.

stem: You review a 60-year-old man who had a drug-eluting stent inserted 6 months ago for ischaemic heart disease. His current medication includes aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, ramipril and bisoprolol. He has developed an inguinal hernia and is keen for surgical repair. The cardiologists plan was to continue clopidogrel for 12 months following stent insertion. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Stop clopidogrel the day before the operation
Stop clopidogrel 7 days before the operation
Stop clopidogrel the day before the operation and start low-molecular weight heparin (prophylaxis dose)
explanation:
Delay operation for 6 months
The correct answer is to delay operation for 6 months. Following insertion of a drug-eluting stent (DES), dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and clopidogrel is essential for 12 months to prevent in-stent thrombosis, which carries a significant mortality risk. The cardiologist's plan to continue clopidogrel for 12 months is in line with current guidelines. Elective surgery should be postponed until completion of this mandatory period of DAPT, as the risk of stent thrombosis outweighs the risk of delaying an inguinal hernia repair.

Stop clopidogrel the day before the operation
Stopping clopidogrel the day before the operation would be dangerous as it takes 5-7 days for the antiplatelet effect to wear off. Additionally, stopping clopidogrel within the crucial 12-month period after DES insertion significantly increases the risk of catastrophic stent thrombosis.

Stop clopidogrel 7 days before the operation
Stopping clopidogrel 7 days before the operation, while allowing adequate time for the antiplatelet effect to wear off, is still inappropriate as it leaves the patient at high risk of stent thrombosis during this early period after DES insertion.

Continue clopidogrel as normal
Continuing clopidogrel as normal would put the patient at significant risk of perioperative bleeding complications during the hernia repair. While this would protect against stent thrombosis, the surgical bleeding risk is unacceptable.

Stop clopidogrel the day before the operation and start low-molecular weight heparin (prophylaxis dose)
Stopping clopidogrel the day before the operation and starting low-molecular weight heparin (prophylaxis dose) is incorrect for two reasons. Firstly, stopping clopidogrel one day before surgery is insufficient for the antiplatelet effect to wear off. Secondly, prophylactic LMWH is not an adequate substitute for DAPT in preventing stent thrombosis, as it works through a different mechanism of action.

stem: Which part of the jugular venous waveform may be exaggerated in tricuspid regurgitation?
explanation:
v wave
The correct answer is the v wave. In tricuspid regurgitation, blood flows back into the right atrium during systole which leads to an increased volume of blood in the atrium. This results in a higher pressure during atrial filling and therefore an exaggerated v wave on the jugular venous waveform.

x descent
The x descent represents atrial relaxation and ventricular contraction. It is not directly affected by tricuspid regurgitation because it doesn't reflect changes in right atrial pressure that occur with this condition.

y descent
The y descent occurs after the v wave and represents rapid emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle following the opening of the tricuspid valve. While this may be affected in some cases of tricuspid regurgitation, it is not typically exaggerated as a result of this condition.

a wave
The a wave represents right atrial contraction. Tricuspid regurgitation does not typically cause an exaggerated a wave because it does not affect atrial contraction.

c wave
The c wave follows the a wave and reflects closure of the tricuspid valve and bulging of it into the right atrium during early ventricular systole. It is not typically exaggerated in tricuspid regurgitation because this condition affects valve function during diastole rather than systole.

stem: A 58-year-old man has 8 months of progressive fatigue and ankle swelling. His past medical history includes an inferior myocardial infarction 2 years ago. His pulse rate is 85 bpm, his BP is 132/75 mmHg, and his oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air. He has a soft pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, a raised jugular venous pressure (JVP) with prominent pulsations, and bilateral pitting oedema to the mid-shins. Non-tender pulsatile hepatomegaly is present. Investigations: NT-proBNP 563 ng/L (< 400) What JVP finding is most likely to be seen?
explanation:
Prominent v wave
Prominent v wave is the correct answer. This patient is likely to have right heart failure secondary to tricuspid regurgitation (TR), as indicated by the pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, raised JVP with prominent pulsations, bilateral pitting oedema, and non-tender pulsatile hepatomegaly. In TR, during ventricular systole, blood flows backwards from the right ventricle into the right atrium.
