Nitroprusside is the preferred drug in a hypertensive emergency. However, in this question, it is mentioned that hydralazine was the only drug available to lower the blood pressure of this patient.

stem: A 24-year-old man attends the clinic with recurrent episodes of collapse. These are often preceded by heart palpitations described as a rapid heart rate. On examination, heart sounds were normal. There was no evidence of heart murmurs, and he was euvolaemic. An ECG is performed in the clinic: ECG Convex ST-segment elevation in V1-V3 followed by a negative T wave; Partial right bundle branch block; QTc 410 ms You order a cardiac genetic panel. A mutation in which gene is expected?
explanation:
SCN5A
Mutations in the SCN5A gene (which encode the myocardial sodium ion channel protein) are the most common gene abnormality seen in Brugada syndrome. The clinical and electrocardiographic features are highly suggestive of Brugada syndrome. A large number of variants exist, however around 20-40% of cases are caused by a mutation in the SCN5A gene which encodes the myocardial sodium ion channel protein.

CAV3
CAV3 is incorrect. Mutations in this gene are associated with hereditary long QT syndrome. The normal QTc makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

MYBPC3
MYBPC3 is incorrect. Nearly 70% of all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) mutations can be found in the sarcomere genes MYH7 and MYBPC3 (encoding for cardiac myosin binding protein C). The ECG features, in this case, are not suggestive of HCM. HCM results in left ventricular hypertrophy, T wave inversion in the precordial leads, and deep, narrow ('dagger-like') Q waves in the lateral (I, aVL, V5-6) +/inferior (II, III, aVF) leads.

MYH7
MYH7 is incorrect. Nearly 70% of all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) mutations can be found in the sarcomere genes MYH7 and MYBPC3 (encoding for cardiac myosin binding protein C). The ECG features, in this case, are not suggestive of HCM (as discussed above).

TTR
TTR is incorrect. Mutations in TTR are associated with transthyretin amyloidosis. Classical electrocardiogram (ECG) findings in cardiac amyloidosis include that of low voltage complexes with increased left ventricular wall thickness on echocardiography. The absence of these features in this case makes cardiac amyloidosis a less likely diagnosis.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with shortness of breath on exertion which has progressively worsened over the last few weeks. On examination his heart rate is regular at 115 beats per minute, blood pressure 125/45 mmHg, and SpO2 94% on room air. On examination, you note bibasal coarse crepitations and an early diastolic murmur. A chest x-ray demonstrates evidence of pulmonary oedema. What condition is associated with the likely underlying cardiac defect?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis
Aortic regurgitation typically causes an early diastolic murmur. The presence of an early diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure make aortic regurgitation (AR) the most likely diagnosis. Causes of AR can be due to valve disease (e.g. bicuspid aortic valve, aortic dissection, spondyloarthropathies (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis) and connective tissue disease) or due to aortic root disease (e.g. rheumatic fever, calcific valve disease, infective endocarditis and connective tissue diseases). Therefore the most likely diagnosis is ankylosing spondylitis.

Down syndrome
Down syndrome classically presents with either an atrial septal defect (soft mid-systolic murmur), VSD (pan systolic murmur) or PDA (continuous murmur).

Noonan syndrome
Most patients with Noonan syndrome have some form of congenital heart disease. The most common heart defect in these individuals is pulmonary valve stenosis which would present with an ejection systolic murmur loudest on inspiration over the pulmonary area.

Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) presents with a raised JVP (with giant v waves), a right ventricular heave, loud P2, and a pan-systolic murmur (i.e. tricuspid regurgitation from PH). Although PH can also present with an early diastolic murmur at the pulmonary area (Graham-Steele murmur) the presence of a wide pulse pressure favour the diagnosis of aortic regurgitation in this case.

Williams syndrome
Williams syndrome is most commonly associated with a supravalvular aortic stenosis which would present with an ejection systolic murmur.

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with breathlessness and leg swelling. She has heart failure (ejection fraction 33%), rheumatoid arthritis and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her medications are 7.5mg bisoprolol once daily, 10mg lisinopril once daily, 20mg furosemide twice daily, 500mg metformin three times daily and 1g paracetamol four times daily. On examination, she has mild bibasal crackles, heart sounds are normal and there is bilateral pedal pitting oedema. Heart rate is 72 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturations are 94% on room air, blood pressure is 124/68mmHg and her temperature is 36.2oC. Bloods from an appointment two weeks previously: Na+ 140 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Bicarbonate 23 mmol/L (22 - 29) Urea 6.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 114 µmol/L (55 - 120) What is the most appropriate medication to start?
explanation:
Spironolactone
Offer a mineralcorticoid receptor antagonist, in addition to an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) and beta-blocker, to people who have heart failure with reduced ejection fraction if they continue to have symptoms of heart failure. Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. According to the NICE guidelines, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist should be started in addition to an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) and beta-blocker, to people who have heart failure with reduced ejection fraction if they continue to have symptoms of heart failure. Serum sodium, potassium, renal function and blood pressure should be measured prior to starting a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and with every dose increase.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is not a first line treatment in heart failure and the decision to prescribe it should only be made in consultation with a cardiology specialist.

Digoxin
The NICE guidelines recommend digoxin if heart failure is worsening or severe, despite first line treatment. As this woman is not on a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, which is part of the first line treatment, she should be prescribed this first.

Ivabradine
Ivabradine can be used in heart failure but the NICE guidelines state that it should not be used if the patient's heart rate is below 75 (it is 72 in the question). Additionally, ivabradine is not first line treatment.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is not typically used in heart failure.

stem: A 43-year-old man who is known to have Wolff-Parkinson White syndrome presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations. He has no other significant history of note. The palpitations started around 4 hours ago and are not associated with chest pain or shortness of breath. On examination blood pressure is 124/80 mmHg and the chest is clear on auscultation. An ECG show atrial fibrillation at a rate of 154 bpm. Of the following options, what is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Flecainide
Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic agent that can be used in patients with Wolff-Parkinson White syndrome to terminate atrial fibrillation. Another option to consider in this situation would be DC cardioversion.

Adenosine
Adenosine should be avoided as blocking the AV node can paradoxically increase ventricular rate resulting in fall in cardiac output.

Verapamil
Verapamil should also be avoided in patients with Wolff-Parkinson White as they may precipitate VT or VF.

Digoxin
Digoxin should also be avoided in patients with Wolff-Parkinson White as they may precipitate VT or VF.

stem: A 68-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 35%) attends a cardiology clinic. He is on optimal medical therapy including an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2-inhibitor, but remains breathless on minimal exertion. Recent upper and lower GI endoscopies were unremarkable. His blood results are shown. Hb 108 g/L (135 - 180) Ferritin 80 ng/mL (30 - 400) Transferrin saturation 15% (20 - 50) What is the most appropriate next step in his management?
explanation:
Intravenous iron infusion
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): iron deficiency should be treated with IV iron therapy if Hb < 150 g/L, once other causes of iron-deficiency have been excluded. Intravenous iron infusion is the correct answer. This patient has symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) despite optimal medical therapy. The blood results show evidence of functional iron deficiency. According to NICE guidelines, patients with HFrEF should be assessed for iron deficiency. Intravenous iron therapy is recommended if their haemoglobin is less than 150 g/L and they have a transferrin saturation (TSAT) below 20% or a ferritin level below 100 ng/mL. This patient meets the criteria with a Hb of 108 g/L, TSAT of 15%, and ferritin of 80 ng/mL. Note that the ferritin threshold is higher than in the general population. IV iron has been shown to improve symptoms, exercise capacity, and quality of life in these patients. As other causes of iron deficiency have been excluded, this is the most appropriate next step.

Arrange a red cell transfusion
Arrange a red cell transfusion is not indicated. Blood transfusion is generally reserved for patients with more severe anaemia (e.g., Hb < 70 g/L) or those who are haemodynamically unstable or have active bleeding. This patient is clinically stable, and his anaemia is not severe enough to warrant the risks associated with transfusion. The primary goal is to replete his iron stores, which is best achieved with iron therapy.

Prescribe oral iron supplements
Prescribe oral iron supplements is a common treatment for iron deficiency but is not the recommended approach in HFrEF. Patients with heart failure often have poor absorption of oral iron from the gut due to mucosal oedema and inflammation. Furthermore, oral iron preparations are frequently associated with gastrointestinal side effects, leading to poor adherence. Clinical trials have demonstrated the superiority of intravenous iron over oral iron or placebo in this patient group.

Switch ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan
Switch ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan is a valid therapeutic step for patients with HFrEF who remain symptomatic despite optimal foundational therapy. However, it is crucial to first address reversible contributing factors to the patient's symptoms. The identified iron deficiency is a treatable condition known to worsen heart failure symptoms. Correcting this is the most appropriate immediate step before escalating other heart failure medications.

Add digoxin
Add digoxin is a second-line therapy for HFrEF, primarily used for symptom control, especially in patients with co-existing atrial fibrillation. It does not improve mortality and does not address the underlying issue of iron deficiency, which is a more specific and treatable cause of this patient's persistent breathlessness. It would be considered only after other therapeutic avenues, including correcting the iron deficiency, have been explored.

stem: You are considering prescribing an antibiotic to a 28-year-old man who tells you he has Long QT syndrome. Which antibiotic is it most important to avoid?
explanation:
Erythromycin
Erythromycin can cause a prolonged QT interval. Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that has been associated with cardiotoxicity, specifically QT interval prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes. This makes it a high-risk medication for patients with Long QT syndrome, who already have an increased risk of these complications. The UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) recommends caution when prescribing drugs known to have this side effect to patients with existing QT interval prolongation.

Doxycycline
Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic and there are no major concerns about its use in patients with Long QT syndrome. While any medication can potentially cause side effects, doxycycline is not generally associated with significant cardiac risks.

Trimethoprim
Trimethoprim is an antibiotic often used for urinary tract infections. It does not typically affect the QT interval significantly and hence is considered safe for use in patients with Long QT syndrome.

Rifampicin
Rifampicin is an antibiotic commonly used in the treatment of tuberculosis. It's also not known to prolong the QT interval or induce ventricular arrhythmias, making it safe for use in these patients.

Co-amoxiclav
Co-amoxiclav, a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, is also not associated with significant cardiotoxicity or QT interval prolongation. Therefore, it too would be considered safe for use in a patient with Long QT syndrome.

stem: A 48-year-old gentleman presents with a 3-day history of palpitations. This is on a background of recurrent atrial fibrillation with previous failed cardioversion attempts but had successful electrical cardioversion 8 months previously. An ECG confirms that he is in atrial fibrillation with a rate of 80 beats per minute. He currently takes bisoprolol and apixaban. The cardiology consultant reviews and has planned electrical cardioversion for 4 weeks time. Until he is cardioverted, which of the following should be given in addition to his current medications?
explanation:
Amiodarone
If high-risk of failure of cardioversion (previous failure), offer electrical cardioversion after at least 4 weeks treatment with amiodarone NICE recommend giving amiodarone or sotalol for at least 4 weeks prior to electrical cardioversion in cases where there is a high risk of failure (recurrent AF or previous failed cardioversion attempts).

Digoxin
Digoxin and verapamil can be used for rate control in AF, but the rate is already well controlled with bisoprolol.

Flecainide
Flecainide can be used for pharmacological cardioversion of AF in patients without structural heart disease, but the question states that electrical cardioversion is planned so there is no role for that here.

Procainamide
Procainamide has a role in ventricular tachycardia but is not indicated here.

Verapamil
Digoxin and verapamil can be used for rate control in AF, but the rate is already well controlled with bisoprolol.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of fever, malaise, and weight loss. He had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 8 months ago. On examination, he has a temperature of 38.5°C and a new diastolic murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transoesophageal echocardiogram shows a vegetation on his prosthetic valve. What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
explanation:
Flucloxacillin + rifampicin + low-dose gentamicin
Flucloxacillin + rifampicin + low-dose gentamicin is the correct treatment for prosthetic valve endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus according to UK guidelines. This patient has clear evidence of prosthetic valve endocarditis with fever, a new murmur, positive blood cultures for S. aureus, and vegetations on echocardiography. The triple therapy approach provides broad coverage and penetration into the biofilm that often forms on prosthetic material. Flucloxacillin is the firstline anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam for methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA). Rifampicin has excellent biofilm penetration, which is crucial for prosthetic material infections. Gentamicin provides synergistic activity against staphylococci. This combination maximizes the chance of eradicating the infection, which carries a high mortality rate of approximately 30% with staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis.

Amoxicillin + low-dose gentamicin
Amoxicillin + low-dose gentamicin would be appropriate initial blind therapy for suspected native valve endocarditis before culture results are available, but is inadequate for confirmed staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis. Amoxicillin does not provide optimal coverage against S. aureus compared to flucloxacillin, and the absence of rifampicin means reduced biofilm penetration.

Benzylpenicillin + low-dose gentamicin
Benzylpenicillin + low-dose gentamicin is the recommended regimen for endocarditis caused by less sensitive streptococci, not for staphylococcal infections. Benzylpenicillin has poor activity against S. aureus, including MSSA strains, making this an inappropriate choice for this patient.

Vancomycin + low-dose gentamicin
Vancomycin + low-dose gentamicin without rifampicin would be suboptimal for prosthetic valve endocarditis. While vancomycin would be appropriate if the patient had a penicillin allergy or if the S. aureus was methicillin-resistant (MRSA), the absence of rifampicin means reduced biofilm penetration, which is crucial in prosthetic valve infections.

Vancomycin + rifampicin
Vancomycin + rifampicin without gentamicin would be appropriate for native valve endocarditis caused by MRSA or in penicillin-allergic patients, but for prosthetic valve endocarditis, the addition of gentamicin is recommended for its synergistic effect, making this regimen incomplete for this clinical scenario.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer is admitted with acute dyspnoea. Her respiratory rate on admission is 42 / min and her oxygen saturations are 87% on room air. A pulmonary embolism is suspected and she is transferred to the high dependency unit after being treated with oxygen and enoxaparin. Which one of the following would be the strongest indication for thrombolysis?
explanation:
Hypotension
Thrombolysis is indicated in patients with pulmonary embolism who are haemodynamically unstable, as evidenced by hypotension. According to the UK guidelines, systemic thrombolysis should be considered for patients with confirmed acute pulmonary embolism and haemodynamic instability (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or a drop in systolic blood pressure of at least 40 mmHg for more than 15 minutes). This is because the presence of hypotension indicates a higher risk of death and adverse outcomes.

Extensive deep venous thrombosis
Extensive deep venous thrombosis is incorrect because although it suggests a higher risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism, it does not necessarily indicate the severity of the pulmonary embolism or the patient's haemodynamic status. Treatment should still follow standard anticoagulation therapy rather than immediate thrombolysis.

Patient choice following informed consent
Patient choice following informed consent is not an appropriate indication for thrombolysis. While patient autonomy and shared decision-making are important aspects of medical care, treatment decisions should be based on clinical evidence and guideline recommendations rather than solely on patient preference.

Hypoxaemia despite high flow oxygen
Hypoxaemia despite high flow oxygen might be concerning, but it does not necessarily warrant thrombolysis. Hypoxaemia can occur due to various factors such as ventilation-perfusion mismatch or shunt effect caused by the pulmonary embolism. Although severe hypoxaemia may indicate a large clot burden, it does not provide information about the patient's haemodynamic stability. Therefore, treatment with anticoagulants remains the first-line approach unless there are other indications for thrombolysis.

ECG showing right ventricular strain
An ECG showing right ventricular strain may suggest that there is significant obstruction in the pulmonary circulation due to the embolism, which can cause an increased workload on the right ventricle. However, this finding alone does not indicate haemodynamic instability or the need for thrombolysis. Management should still focus on standard anticoagulation therapy unless other criteria for thrombolysis are met.

stem: A 28-year-old female who is known to be 16 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department with a 4-day history of leg pain. She reports a progressive aching and swelling of her right calf. The patient is otherwise well and denies any other symptoms General examination is normal, and observations are all within normal range. On examination of the affected leg the right calf is swollen >3cm compared to the left which localised tenderness along on deep palpation of the calf. There are collateral superficial veins as well as pitting oedema also noted on the affected leg. What is the mechanism of action of the treatment most appropriate to commence in this patient?
options: Activated antithrombin I which inhibits of factor Xa, IXa, Xia and XIIa
Activated antithrombin III which inhibits factor Xa
Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase which inhibits vitamin K1
explanation:
Activated antithrombin III which inhibits factor Xa
Low-molecular weight heparin activates antithrombin III. Forms a complex that inhibits factor Xa. This patient has presented with typical signs and symptoms in keeping with a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Pregnancy can result in an increased hypercoagulable state and therefore patients are more at risk of forming these DVTs. In standard cases, there are a variety of treatment options available to manage DVTs long term including warfarin, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin. Only low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) has been recommended for use in pregnancy due to the potential or confirmed teratogenic properties of the other treatment options. LMWH activates antithrombin III which inhibits factor Xa only, bringing about a breakdown in clot formation.

Activated antithrombin I which inhibits of factor Xa, IXa, Xia and XIIa
Standard heparin is useful for thrombosis management in situations where there is a high risk of bleeding or in renal impairment due to its short half-life. It works by activating antithrombin III (not antithrombin I) which inhibits a number of factors including Xa, IXa, Xia and XIIa. Heparin must be given intravenously and therefore is less appropriate than LMWH, which can be given subcutaneously.

Directly inhibits factor Xa
DOACs which can be used in DVT management directly inhibit factor Xa, breaking down clot formation. The teratogenic profile of DOACs are unknown and therefore, to date are not advised in pregnancy, with LMWH being the preferred option.

Inhibits cyclooxygenases (COX) reducing platelets aggregation
One of aspirin's main mechanisms of action is the inhibition of COX 1 and 2 which inhibits platelet aggregation. Although used to reduce the risk of some thrombosis conditions including acute coronary syndrome and stroke aspirin has no role in the management of DVTs.

Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase which inhibits vitamin K1
Warfarin causes the breakdown of clot formation by blocking vitamin K epoxide reductase which is required to reactivate vitamin K1. Without active vitamin K1 several clotting factors including II, VII, IX and X have reduced function. Warfarin can be used in the management of a DVT however it is teratogenic causing foetal warfarin syndrome with characteristic abnormalities including, birth weight issues, central nervous system issues and malformation of bones, cartilage and joints.

stem: A 56-year-old Asian man presented with chest pain to the emergency department. He was diagnosed with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction following initial investigations. He was treated with dual antiplatelet therapy, with both aspirin and ticagrelor, as well as subcutaneous fondaparinux. A few days after starting the treatment he reported feeling short of breath. What is the mechanism of the action of the offending drug in this case?
options: Inhibits ADP binding to platelet receptors
explanation:
Inhibits ADP binding to platelet receptors
Ticagrelor has a similar mechanism of action to clopidogrel and inhibits ADP binding to platelet receptors. Ticagrelor is a P2Y12 receptor antagonist that prevents ADP-mediated P2Y12 dependent platelet activation and aggregation. The sensation of dyspnoea in ticagrelor-treated patients is triggered by adenosine. Ticagrelor prevents the clearance of adenosine, which increases its concentration in the circulation. Adenosine receptors are found in the lungs, where adenosine has been shown to stimulate sensory nerve fibres that can produce dyspnoea.

Xa inhibitor
Fondaparinux is a factor Xa inhibitor. Other examples of factor Xa inhibitors include rivaroxaban and apixaban. Common side effects include easy bruising and bleeding. Dyspnoea could occur in the event of severe blood loss or pulmonary, but neither of these have been suggested here.

COX-1 inhibitor
Aspirin works by blocking prostaglandin synthesis. It is non-selective for COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. Aspirin commonly causes side effects such as gastric irritation, heartburn, and bleeding. None of the medications listed has a selective mechanism of action for COX-1.

Non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor
Aspirin works by blocking prostaglandin synthesis. It is non-selective for COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes. Aspirin commonly causes side effects such as gastric irritation, heartburn, and bleeding. None of the medications listed has a selective mechanism of action for COX-1 or COX-2.

COX-2 inhibitor
None of the medications listed has a selective mechanism of action for COX-1 or COX-2.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department following a collapse. He states that he became lightheaded whilst on a jog. This has happened on two occasions previously. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medicines (including over-the-counter and herbal supplements). Blood results are as follows: Na+ 136 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Calcium 2.4 mmol/L (2.1-2.6) Phosphate 0.9 mmol/L (0.8-1.4) Magnesium 0.75 mmol/L (0.7-1.0) An ECG is performed in the department: ECG Sinus rhythm with a rate of 74 beats per minute; markedly prolonged QTc 540ms What is the most likely abnormality?
explanation:
Loss-of-function of K+ channels
Long QT syndrome - usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels. The most common variants of LQTS (LQT1 & LQT2) are caused by defects in the alpha subunit of the slow delayed rectifier K+ channel resulting in loss-of-function of K+ channels.

Gain-of-function of K+ channels
Long QT syndrome is usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels, not gain-of-function.

Gain-of-function of Na+ channels
Long QT syndrome is usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels, not gain-of-function of Na+ channels.

Loss-of-function of Ca2+ channels
Long QT syndrome is usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels, not loss-of-function of Ca2+ channels.

Loss-of-function of Na+ channels
Long QT syndrome is usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels, not loss-of-function of Na+ channels.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is referred to cardiology outpatients with palpitations. She has no significant past medical history. On examination, she has a fixed, widely split second heart sound and a grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur heard loudest at the upper left sternal edge. The murmur increases in intensity during inspiration. Her ECG shows right bundle branch block. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Atrial septal defect
Atrial septal defect is the correct diagnosis based on the clinical findings. The patient presents with a fixed, widely split second heart sound, which is characteristic of atrial septal defect (ASD). This occurs because the right ventricular volume overload leads to delayed right ventricular emptying, causing persistent splitting of S2 that doesn't vary with respiration. The ejection systolic murmur heard at the upper left sternal edge that increases with inspiration is due to increased flow across the pulmonary valve (relative pulmonary stenosis). This is a right-sided murmur, and right-sided murmurs classically increase during inspiration due to increased venous return to the right heart. The right bundle branch block on ECG is also consistent with ASD, as the increased right ventricular volume leads to right ventricular conduction delay. The young age of the patient and presentation with palpitations are also typical for ASD.

Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is incorrect. Mitral regurgitation produces a pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur best heard at the apex and radiating to the axilla. Being a left-sided murmur, it would typically decrease in intensity during inspiration rather than increase. Additionally, mitral regurgitation would not cause a fixed, widely split second heart sound or right bundle branch block on ECG.

Patent ductus arteriosus
Patent ductus arteriosus is incorrect. PDA typically produces a continuous 'machinery' murmur that persists throughout systole and diastole, best heard in the left infraclavicular area. It would not cause a fixed, widely split second heart sound, and the murmur would not characteristically increase with inspiration as it is primarily a left-sided lesion.

Pulmonary stenosis
Pulmonary stenosis can produce an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge that increases with inspiration, similar to ASD. However, pulmonary stenosis typically causes an ejection click followed by the murmur, and the second heart sound would be widely split but not fixed (it would still vary with respiration). The absence of an ejection click and the presence of fixed splitting of S2 make pulmonary stenosis less likely than ASD.

Ventricular septal defect
Ventricular septal defect produces a pansystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal edge. The murmur is typically harsh in character and does not vary significantly with respiration as it is primarily a left-to-right shunt. VSD does not cause fixed splitting of S2, and small VSDs (more common in adults) typically cause a louder murmur than larger ones due to the greater pressure gradient across a smaller defect.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with a history of chronic kidney disease stage 4 and metastatic breast cancer is admitted with a swollen right calf. Investigations confirm a deep vein thrombosis and she is started on treatment dose dalteparin. As she has a significant degree of renal impairment it is decided to monitor her response to dalteparin. What is the most appropriate blood test to perform?
explanation:
Anti-Factor Xa levels
The correct answer is Anti-Factor Xa levels. In patients with renal impairment, monitoring the response to low molecular weight heparins (LMWH) like dalteparin is essential to ensure appropriate anticoagulation and minimize the risk of bleeding. Anti-Factor Xa levels are the most appropriate blood test to perform in this situation as they directly measure the activity of LMWH and provide an accurate assessment of their anticoagulant effect.

Antithrombin III levels
Antithrombin III levels are not a useful test for monitoring LMWH therapy. Antithrombin III is a naturally occurring anticoagulant protein that inhibits several coagulation factors, including factor Xa. While LMWHs exert their anticoagulant effect by enhancing the activity of antithrombin III, measuring its levels will not provide information about the efficacy of dalteparin therapy.

Anti-Factor VIIIa levels
Anti-Factor VIIIa levels are also not helpful in monitoring dalteparin therapy. Factor VIIIa is involved in the intrinsic pathway of coagulation and has no direct interaction with LMWHs. Therefore, assessing antiFactor VIIIa levels will not provide any insight into the patient's response to dalteparin.

Prothrombin time (PT)
Prothrombin time (PT) measures the extrinsic pathway and common pathway of coagulation and is used primarily for monitoring warfarin therapy. It is not sensitive enough to detect changes in response to LMWH treatment, making it an inappropriate choice for monitoring dalteparin therapy in this patient.

Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT)
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) assesses the intrinsic pathway and common pathway of coagulation. While it can be used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy, it does not accurately reflect LMWH activity due to their different mechanisms of action on antithrombin III. Therefore, APTT is not the most appropriate test for monitoring dalteparin therapy in this patient.

stem: You get bleeped in the middle of your night shift to talk to a worried father whose daughter has been admitted with cyanosis. He tells you that they were aware she has had a murmur since birth, but it has only been the last few days in which she has had symptoms. You believe that this is a case of Eisenmenger's syndrome. What is the medical definition of Eisenmenger's syndrome?
options: The reversal of a right-to-left shunt
Presence of a ventricular septal defect alongside an atrial septal defect
The reversal of a left-to-right shunt
All four of the following: overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular septal defect
explanation:
The reversal of a left-to-right shunt
Eisenmenger's syndrome is the reversal of a left-to-right shunt associated with ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus.

The reversal of a right-to-left shunt
The reversal of a right-to-left shunt is not the correct definition. Eisenmenger's syndrome specifically involves the reversal of a left-to-right shunt.

All four of the following: overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular septal defect
Eisenmenger's syndrome does not include all four of the following: overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, and ventricular septal defect. It specifically involves the reversal of a left-to-right shunt.

stem: You are working a medical ward cover shift when a crash call is put out for a 64-year-old man arrested on the ward. He was admitted this morning with acute breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain and is being treated as a likely pulmonary embolus with treatment-dose dalteparin whilst he awaits his CT pulmonary angiogram. When you arrive, the first cycle of cardiopulmonary resuscitation is underway. He has a laryngeal mask airway in situ with good effect. After 2 minutes of chest compressions, the defibrillator shows normal sinus rhythm. He does not have a palpable central pulse. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
explanation:
Adrenaline 1mg 1:10000
ALS - give adrenaline in non-shockable rhythm as soon as possible. This patient's rhythm demonstrated on the defibrillator is pulseless electrical activity (PEA). It is a non-shockable rhythm, and therefore adrenaline should be given immediately. The cardiac arrest dose of adrenaline is 1mg 1:10000.

Intravenous fluids
Intravenous fluids are used in a cardiac arrest to correct hypovolaemia (one of the 4Hs and 4Ts). However, it is not the most immediate treatment to give.

Adrenaline 1mg 1:1000
Adrenaline 1mg 1:1000 is incorrect. Although the dose of 1mg is correct, a 1:1000 preparation is not what is used in a cardiac arrest. A 500 microgram 1:1000 dose is used in the treatment of anaphylaxis.

Alteplase 50mg
Alteplase can be given if a massive pulmonary embolus is expected. However, adrenaline takes priority during a cardiac arrest scenario.

Unsynchronised 150J shock
An unsynchronised 150J shock would be the next correct step if this patient were in a shockable rhythm such as pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. However, this patient's rhythm is PEA making adrenaline the correct choice.

stem: A 64-year-old man is reviewed in the cardiology clinic. He has a history of stable angina, for which he currently takes bisoprolol, amlodipine and isosorbide mononitrate. Despite this, he continues to experience chest pain on exertion. After further discussion, the cardiologist decides to offer the patient a trial of nicorandil. He explains the side effect profile of the drug to the patient, including its ability to cause ulceration in the gastrointestinal tract. Where might this ulceration occur?
explanation:
Anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract
Nicorandil may cause ulceration anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract. The correct answer is anywhere along the tract. Nicorandil is known to cause ulceration of the gastrointestinal tract, although this is not as common as its other side effects - dizziness, nausea, vomiting and headache. This ulceration may occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract.

Lower gastrointestinal tract
For this reason, the other options are incorrect, as they all specify specific regions of the tract.

Mouth and oesophagus
For this reason, the other options are incorrect, as they all specify specific regions of the tract.

Stomach and duodenum
For this reason, the other options are incorrect, as they all specify specific regions of the tract.

Upper gastrointestinal tract
For this reason, the other options are incorrect, as they all specify specific regions of the tract.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic with recurrent episodes of central tight chest pain for the past 3 months. The pain often occurs during physical activity but also at rest. The following investigations are performed: Electrocardiogram (ECG) No signs of acute ischaemia Echocardiogram Unremarkable Stress test ST-segment depression, correlating with patient's reported symptoms Coronary angiography No significant coronary artery stenosis or obstructive disease; Notably the patient had chest pain at the time of the procedure What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Syndrome X
Based on the patient's symptoms, stress test results, and the findings from advanced imaging techniques, the most likely diagnosis is microvascular angina, also known as Syndrome X. People with cardiac syndrome X have normal coronary angiograms despite ECG changes on exercise stress testing.

Angina
The absence of stenosis or obstructive disease on angiography makes angina a less likely diagnosis.

Coronary bridging
The normal coronary angiography makes coronary bridging a less likely diagnosis. During angiography, the compression of the artery can be observed, and the degree of narrowing or compression during systole can be quantified.

Coronary vasospasm
Coronary angiography during an episode of spasm may show transient narrowing of the coronary arteries. Since the patient was symptomatic at the time of a normal coronary angiography, vasospasm is a less likely diagnosis.

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Echocardiography is often used to diagnose and evaluate the extent of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. It can show characteristic changes in the heart's contraction pattern, such as a ballooning or 'apical ballooning' appearance of the left ventricle, which resembles a Takotsubo (a Japanese octopus trap, which gives the condition its name). The normal echo makes Takotsubo cardiomyopathy an unlikely diagnosis.

stem: A 52-year-old lorry driver presents to cardiology clinic with a history of recurrent palpitations. He has had three episodes of ventricular tachycardia in the past year, all requiring emergency cardioversion. After discussion with the multidisciplinary team, an implantable cardioverterdefibrillator (ICD) is recommended. The patient is concerned about the impact on his career. What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving licence?
options: He can continue driving lorries after a 6-month suspension
He can continue driving lorries after a 1-month suspension
He can continue driving lorries immediately after ICD implantation
He must surrender his lorry driving licence permanently
He can continue driving lorries if he remains arrhythmia-free for 12 months
explanation:
He must surrender his lorry driving licence permanently
ICD means loss of HGV licence, regardless of the circumstances. He must surrender his lorry driving licence permanently is the correct answer. According to DVLA guidelines, the implantation of an ICD results in a permanent bar for Group 2 licence holders, which includes heavy goods vehicle (HGV) drivers. This is regardless of the indication for ICD implantation (whether for secondary prevention following documented arrhythmia or for primary prevention). The restriction is in place due to the significant risk to public safety if a professional driver were to experience an arrhythmia or ICD discharge while operating a large vehicle. The patient should be advised that he will need to surrender his Group 2 licence permanently once the ICD is implanted. He should be informed of this significant career implication before proceeding with the implantation.

He can continue driving lorries after a 6-month suspension
He can continue driving lorries after a 6-month suspension is incorrect. While patients with ICDs who hold standard Group 1 licences (for cars and motorcycles) must cease driving for 6 months if the device was implanted following a sustained ventricular arrhythmia, this rule does not apply to Group 2 licence holders. For lorry drivers, the restriction is permanent rather than temporary.

He can continue driving lorries after a 1-month suspension
He can continue driving lorries after a 1-month suspension is incorrect. The 1-month driving suspension applies only to Group 1 licence holders (cars and motorcycles) who have had an ICD implanted prophylactically. For Group 2 licence holders like this patient, ICD implantation results in permanent licence revocation regardless of the circumstances.

He can continue driving lorries immediately after ICD implantation
He can continue driving lorries immediately after ICD implantation is incorrect. There is no scenario in which immediate return to driving lorries after ICD implantation is permitted under DVLA guidelines. This would pose a significant risk to public safety.

He can continue driving lorries if he remains arrhythmia-free for 12 months
He can continue driving lorries if he remains arrhythmia-free for 12 months is incorrect. Remaining arrhythmia-free for any period does not change the permanent restriction on Group 2 licences following ICD implantation. The presence of the device itself, regardless of whether it has needed to deliver therapy, is the determining factor for the permanent driving restriction.

stem: Which of the following is not true regarding B-type natriuretic peptide?
options: Levels rise in left ventricular failure
explanation:
Acts as a vasoconstrictor
The correct answer is vasoconstrictor as this is not a true characteristic of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). BNP is actually a potent vasodilator, which helps reduce cardiac preload and afterload in heart failure. This vasodilatory effect, combined with its other actions, makes it an important compensatory mechanism in cardiac dysfunction.

Secreted mainly by the ventricles
Secreted mainly by the ventricles is correct - BNP is primarily synthesized and released by ventricular myocytes in response to increased wall stretch and volume overload.

Acts as a diuretic
Acts as a diuretic is correct - BNP promotes natriuresis and diuresis by increasing glomerular filtration rate and inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the kidneys.

Levels rise in left ventricular failure
Levels rise in left ventricular failure is correct - BNP levels increase significantly in response to ventricular wall stress and are used as a diagnostic marker for heart failure.

Reduces sympathetic tone
Reduces sympathetic tone is correct - BNP has inhibitory effects on the sympathetic nervous system, helping to reduce the excessive neurohormonal activation seen in heart failure.

stem: A 56-year-old man presented with worsening central chest pain radiating down his left arm associated with difficulty in breathing and nausea. He was diagnosed with an inferior myocardial infarction. Following his recovery in the coronary care unit with serial electrocardiography monitoring, he found to be in a complete heart block. He denies any symptoms from this. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
Conservative monitoring
Complete heart block following an inferior MI is NOT an indication for pacing, unlike with an anterior MI. Complete (third-degree atrioventricular) heart blocks are commonly seen with inferior wall myocardial infarctions and usually resolve in hours to days after revascularization. Right coronary artery occlusion is usually implicated as it vascularises the AV nodal artery. Bradyarrhythmias and AV block in the context of inferior STEMI are usually transient (lasting hours to days), respond well to atropine and do not require permanent or temporary pacing especially if haemodynamically stable and asymptomatic.

Atropine
Atropine aims to improve conduction through the AVN by reducing vagal tone via receptor blockade. It is often indicated in symptomatic patients and would not be needed in this case.

Isoprenaline
Isoprenaline is used to maintain heart rate temporarily in patients with heart block only until a temporary or permanent pacemaker can be fitted. It is usually given as an intravenous infusion under ECG control but would not be indicated in this case.

Pacemaker insertion
Permanent pacing is the routine treatment for irreversible third-degree and advanced second-degree atrioventricular (AV) block but in cases such as this where the blockage is transient permanent pacemakers are rarely required.

Temporary pacing
Temporary pacing may be required if the patient was symptomatic or with haemodynamically unstable bradycardia, not responding to atropine.

stem: A 41-year-old male is diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. He undergoes vasodilator testing with intravenous epoprostenol to which he has a positive response. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for his condition?
explanation:
Nifedipine
Pulmonary arterial hypertension patients with positive response to vasodilator testing should be treated with calcium channel blockers. Patients who test positive to vasodilator testing are typically treated with calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine, diltiazem and increasingly amlodipine, making option 5 the correct answer.

Sildenafil
Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor used in patients who test negative to vasodilators.

Treprostinil
Treprostinil is a prostacyclin analogue used in patients who do not respond to acute vasodilator testing.

Bosentan
Bosentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist also used for patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension who are negative during vasodilator testing.

Isosorbide mononitrate
Isosorbide mononitrate is used in the treatment of angina not pulmonary arterial hypertension.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents to his general practitioner for a routine health check. He feels generally well in himself; he has a past medical history of hypertension and angina. His regular medications include ramipril, amlodipine, bisoprolol, isosorbide mononitrate and nicorandil. The examination is unremarkable, although he explains that the dentist recently noted overgrowth of his gums. What medication is most likely to be causing this effect?
explanation:
Amlodipine
Amlodipine may cause gingival hyperplasia. Several drugs are typically associated with gingival hyperplasia. Classically, phenytoin, cyclosporin and calcium-channel blockers are linked to this side effect. As such, amlodipine is the correct answer here. Nifedipine is more commonly associated with gingival hyperplasia, although amlodipine is also known to cause it.

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker, used here in the management of this patient's hypertension/angina. It is not linked to gingival hyperplasia.

Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN)
Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN) is used in the management of this patient's angina. It is not associated with gingival hyperplasia.

Nicorandil
Nicorandil is an anti-anginal drug often used when initial measures have not been adequate. It is not linked with gingival hyperplasia. However, it is associated with oral ulceration and, indeed, ulceration anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract.

Ramipril
Ramipril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor used to manage hypertension. It is not linked to gingival hyperplasia.

stem: You are a doctor on the medical assessment unit. You are asked to review a 52-year-old man with a past medical history of prostate cancer for which he is on goserelin injections. He was admitted from the emergency department requiring 35% oxygen to maintain saturations >94%. He describes a one week history of gradually worsening dyspnoea and dizziness. He denies a persistent cough but states he has had two episodes of frank haemoptysis. He denied collapse and loss of consciousness. Arterial blood gas (ABG) on room air: pH 7.540 (7.350 - 7.450) pCO2 2.56 kPa (4.60 - 6.00) pO2 9.66kPa (11.0 - 14.4) Bicarbonate 16.6 mmol/L (18.0 - 28.0) Echocardiogram Adequate left ventricular systolic function with ejection fraction >55%. Right ventricular enlargement with estimated PASP (pulmonary arterial systolic pressure) of 44mmHg (not including right atrial pressure). Evidence of right atrial enlargement. What is the most likely cardiovascular abnormality to be found on auscultation?
explanation:
Loud S2 heart sound
Pulmonary hypertension is a cause of a loud S2 (due to a loud P2). Given the above patient's history along with findings of a respiratory alkalosis with partial metabolic compensation on an ABG, a pulmonary embolism is likely. This is of further concern given evidence of increased right heart pressures on echocardiogram. Given the likelihood of pulmonary embolism plus high right-sided heart pressures, pulmonary hypertension is the most likely finding and thus a loud S2.

Ejection systolic murmur
Ejection systolic murmur is most commonly heard in aortic and pulmonary stenosis. Aortic stenosis is the most common murmur to be heard in clinical examination and can be heard radiating into the carotids. Aortic sclerosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also cause an ejection systolic murmur but these do not radiate into the carotid arteries.

Soft S2 heart sound
Soft S2 heart sound can also be split into soft A2 and P2. Soft A2 can be heard in aortic regurgitation and stenosis, whilst soft P2 may be heard in pulmonary stenosis.

S3 heart sound
S3 heart sound (ventricular gallop rhythm) is due to rapid ventricular filling after opening of the atrioventricular valves. It is normal to be heard in children and pregnant women. Pathological causes include mitral regurgitation and left ventricular failure.

S4 heart sound
S4 heart sound (atrial gallop rhythm) occurs at the end of diastole prior to S1. It is caused by left ventricular hypertrophy and failure and can be heard in hypertension, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and aortic stenosis.

stem: A 28-year-old man who is normally fit and well presents with palpitations. He has no chest pain. Apart from tachycardia his examination is unremarkable. His blood pressure is 105/70mmHg and his heart rate is 170 beats/min and regular. An electrocardiogram (ECG) is completed: ECG Rate 170 beats/min, regular, QRS 140ms with uniform appearance, right bundle branch pattern. There is no previous ECG to compare to. Which drug, if given, is most likely to precipitate severe hypotension, ventricular fibrillation or cardiac arrest in this patient and should therefore be avoided?
explanation:
Verapamil
Verapamil is an option for termination of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). However, it should be avoided here as we do not know for certain whether this is SVT or VT. If it is VT, verapamil may precipitate cardiac arrest.

Adenosine
Although not advised by Resuscitation Council guidelines, adenosine is felt to be safe to give in broad complex tachycardia and some guidelines advise it can help diagnosis if it corrects the rhythm, although this is controversial as some ventricular tachycardias will respond to adenosine. (Adenosine should however definitely be avoided in irregular broad complex tachycardia as it can precipitate ventricular fibrillation).

Amiodarone
Amiodarone, lidocaine and procainamide are all potential therapeutic options for ventricular tachycardia in this patient without structural heart disease.

Lidocaine
Amiodarone, lidocaine and procainamide are all potential therapeutic options for ventricular tachycardia in this patient without structural heart disease.

Procainamide
Amiodarone, lidocaine and procainamide are all potential therapeutic options for ventricular tachycardia in this patient without structural heart disease.

stem: You are asked to review a 63-year-old woman admitted to your ward with a lower respiratory tract infection. She has a past medical history of gout and hypertension. Her medications consist of amlodipine 10mg once daily and allopurinol 100mg once daily. You note that her blood pressure over the last three days has been persistently elevated. The last three readings were: 149/76 mmHg 158/88 mmHg 150/82 mmHg Which of the following antihypertensive medications would be the most appropriate to start?
explanation:
Lisinopril
Given that this patient is already on a calcium channel-blocker and continues to have uncontrolled hypertension, it is appropriate to commence an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker (ARB). Of the above medications, lisinopril is correct.

Atenolol
Atenolol would be appropriate if the patient was on a calcium channel blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARB and thiazide-like diuretic with a potassium >4.5 mmol/L.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide and indapamide are thiazide-like diuretics which should be considered if a patient is on a calcium channel blockers and ACE inhibitor/ARB. Also, given this patient's history of gout, thiazide-like diuretics increase the risk of exacerbations of gout.

Spironolactone
Spironolactone should be considered if the patient was on a calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitor/ARB and thiazide-like diuretic with a potassium <4.5 mmol/L.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a broad complex tachycardia. Which of the following features would make it more likely that this was due to a supraventricular tachycardia rather than a ventricular tachycardia?
options: Absence of QRS concordance in chest leads
explanation:
Absence of QRS concordance in chest leads
Positive QRS concordance in the chest leads is associated with ventricular tachycardia. Therefore, the absence of QRS concordance in chest leads makes it more likely that the tachycardia is supraventricular.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and episodes of dizziness. On examination, he has a late-peaking systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border with radiation to the carotids. There is an associated slow-rising carotid pulse. An echocardiography confirms the diagnosis. What is the most likely underlying cause of his condition?
explanation:
Degenerative tri-leaflet aortic valve stenosis
The physical examination findings are highly suggestive of aortic stenosis: late-peaking systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border with radiation to the carotids, associated slow-rising carotid pulse. In patients over 65, the most common cause of aortic stenosis is degenerative calcification of a normal trileaflet aortic valve. This process is driven by age-related changes, chronic mechanical stress, and risk factors similar to atherosclerosis (e.g., hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes).

Congenital bicuspid aortic valve stenosis
A bicuspid aortic valve is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in younger patients (< 65 years). It predisposes to earlier degeneration and calcification due to abnormal valve anatomy and increased mechanical stress. While this could occur in an older patient, the most likely cause in this age group is the calcification of a normal tri-leaflet valve.

Congenital pulmonary valve stenosis
Even though the murmur can be similar to aortic valve stenosis, pulmonary stenosis is very rare in the elderly population.

Degenerative mitral valve regurgitation
Degenerative mitral valve regurgitation is a common valvular dysfunction in elderly patients. However, this patient lacks clinical features suggestive of mitral regurgitation (a pansystolic murmur heard best at the apex).

Rheumatic mitral valve stenosis
Rheumatic fever can cause valve disease but more commonly it affects the mitral valve. The physical examination findings in the scenario do not suggest mitral stenosis (low-pitched decrescendo-crescendo rumbling diastolic murmur). In addition, rheumatic valve disease is rare in developed countries.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation collapses in the antenatal clinic. She is unresponsive with no palpable pulse. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is commenced immediately. The cardiac monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. A defibrillator is being prepared. Which additional intervention is most important to optimise the effectiveness of resuscitation in this patient?
options: Position in full left lateral position
explanation:
Position with 15° left lateral tilt
In pregnant women beyond 20 weeks' gestation undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation, a left lateral tilt of approximately 15° is essential to prevent aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus. The enlarged uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when the patient is supine, significantly reducing venous return and cardiac output, thereby reducing the effectiveness of chest compressions. This positioning is typically achieved by placing a firm wedge, pillow, or folded towels under the right hip or buttock, allowing effective chest compressions whilst relieving caval compression. This patient at 28 weeks' gestation requires this specific positioning to optimise resuscitation outcomes.

Position with 15° head-up tilt
A head-up tilt would not address the issue of aortocaval compression in pregnancy and would potentially reduce cerebral perfusion during cardiac arrest, which is detrimental during resuscitation.

Position with 15° right lateral tilt
Tilting to the right would worsen aortocaval compression as the gravid uterus would be positioned directly over the inferior vena cava, further compromising venous return during resuscitation.

Position supine with legs elevated
Whilst leg elevation may be used in some shock states, it does not address the specific problem of aortocaval compression in late pregnancy and would not optimise resuscitation effectiveness in this scenario.

Position in full left lateral position
A full lateral position would make effective chest compressions technically impossible. The 15° tilt provides the optimal balance between relieving caval compression whilst maintaining a position that allows high-quality chest compressions to be delivered.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to a rural hospital with one hour of central chest pain. An ECG confirms an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The nearest percutaneous coronary intervention centre is over two hours away, so a decision is made to administer intravenous alteplase. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Blocks the P2Y12 receptor on platelets
Catalyses the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin
Potentiates the action of antithrombin III
explanation:
Catalyses the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin
Thrombolytic drugs act as tissue plasminogen activators, converting plasminogen into plasmin. Catalyses the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin is the correct answer. Alteplase is a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). In the context of an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), its purpose is to dissolve the occlusive fibrin thrombus in the coronary artery. It achieves this by acting as a powerful enzyme that converts plasminogen, an inactive proenzyme circulating in the blood, into its active form, plasmin. Plasmin is a serine protease that degrades the fibrin meshwork of the clot, leading to thrombolysis and restoration of blood flow to the ischaemic myocardium.

Blocks the P2Y12 receptor on platelets
Blocks the P2Y12 receptor on platelets describes the mechanism of drugs such as clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticagrelor. These are antiplatelet agents used in the management of acute coronary syndromes to prevent further platelet aggregation. While they are a key part of treatment, they do not actively dissolve an existing thrombus and are not thrombolytic agents.

Directly inhibits factor Xa
Directly inhibits factor Xa is the mechanism of action for direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) like apixaban and rivaroxaban. These drugs prevent the propagation of thrombus by inhibiting a key enzyme in the common coagulation pathway. They are used for anticoagulation in conditions like atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism but are not used for thrombolysis in acute STEMI.

Irreversibly inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-1
Irreversibly inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-1 is the mechanism of action of aspirin. By inhibiting the COX-1 enzyme in platelets, aspirin prevents the formation of thromboxane A2, a potent stimulator of platelet aggregation. A loading dose of aspirin is given immediately in suspected STEMI, but its role is antiplatelet, not thrombolytic.

Potentiates the action of antithrombin III
Potentiates the action of antithrombin III is the mechanism of heparins (both unfractionated and low-molecular-weight). By enhancing the activity of antithrombin III, heparins inactivate thrombin (factor IIa) and factor Xa. Heparin is given as an adjunct to thrombolysis to prevent re-occlusion and further clot formation, but it does not have a direct fibrinolytic effect.

stem: A 56-year-old man with a past history of ischaemic heart disease is admitted with central chest pain radiating to his left arm associated with nausea. On arrival in the Coronary Care Unit he is noted to be in complete heart block. Which coronary artery is likely to be affected?
explanation:
Right coronary
The right coronary artery supplies the atrioventricular node in 90% of patients.

stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted with palpitations. During examination of his JVP he is noted to have regular cannon waves. Which one of the following arrhythmias is most likely to be responsible for this finding?
explanation:
Atrio-ventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia
Atrio-ventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia and ventricular tachycardia with 1:1 ventricular-atrial conduction may produce regular cannon waves.

Complete heart block
Complete heart block causes irregular cannon waves.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with aortic dissection?
explanation:
Bicuspid aortic valve
A bicuspid aortic valve increases the risk of aortic dissection six-fold.

stem: A 76-year-old gentleman is admitted through the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath and ankle swelling on a background of left ventricular failure secondary to ischaemic heart disease. He has bibasal crepitations on auscultation and a raised JVP of 4 cm with peripheral pitting oedema to his knees. He is commenced on IV furosemide. What is the mechanism of action of furosemide?
options: Inhibition of the Na+Cl- transporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter in the proximal tubule
Inhibition of sodium channels in the collecting tubules
explanation:
Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Furosemide - inhibits the Na-K-Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) act by inhibiting the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. This causes loss of water along with sodium chloride, potassium, calcium, and hydrogen ions.

Inhibition of the Na+Cl- transporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Describes mechanism of thiazide diuretics

Aldosterone antagonist
Spironolactone and eplerenone are examples of aldosterone antagonists

Inhibition of the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter in the proximal tubule
This answer is incorrect

Inhibition of sodium channels in the collecting tubules
Describes mechanism of amiloride and triamterene.

stem: Which one of the following features would indicate cardiac tamponade rather than constrictive pericarditis?
explanation:
No Y descent on JVP
In cardiac tamponade there is characteristically no Y descent on the JVP.

Raised JVP
The other four features are seen in both cardiac tamponade and constrictive pericarditis

Muffled heart sounds
The other four features are seen in both cardiac tamponade and constrictive pericarditis

Hypotension
The other four features are seen in both cardiac tamponade and constrictive pericarditis

Tachycardia
The other four features are seen in both cardiac tamponade and constrictive pericarditis.

stem: A 28-year-old man with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is investigated for palpitations. A 24 hour ECG reveals runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Implantable cardioverter defibrillator
Most cardiologists would now proceed to inserting an implantable cardioverter defibrillator to lower the risk of sudden cardiac death.

stem: Which of the following is least likely to be a precipitating factor in digoxin toxicity?
explanation:
Hypocalcaemia
Hyper-, not hypocalcaemia may be a precipitating factor in digoxin toxicity.

stem: A 60-year-old man is admitted with palpitations to the Emergency Department. An ECG on admission shows a broad complex tachycardia at a rate of 150 bpm. His blood pressure is 124/82 mmHg and there is no evidence of heart failure. Which one of the following is it least appropriate to give?
explanation:
Verapamil
Verapamil should never be given to a patient with a broad complex tachycardia as it may precipitate ventricular fibrillation in patients with ventricular tachycardia.

Adenosine
Adenosine is sometimes given in this situation as a 'trial' if there is a strong suspicion the underlying rhythm is a supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction.

stem: A 73 year-old male has progressive exertional dyspnoea due to progressive systolic heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. What investigation is most useful in predicting symptomatic response to cardiac resynchronisation therapy?
explanation:
ECG
The key diagnostic tests used to identify patients likely to benefit from cardiac resynchronization therapy is the transthoracic echocardiogram and ECG. Those with left ventricular ejection fractions of <35% and a LBBB (QRS duration greater than 120 ms) on ECG are excellent candidates for CRT (biventricular pacing).

Cardiac MRI
null

Transoesophageal Echo
A transoesophageal echo is not required.

Coronary angiogram
null

Nuclear perfusion scan
null.

stem: A 48-year-old Asian lady was seen by her general practitioner (GP) with a 3-week history of fever, fatigue and night sweats. On examination, she was found to have absent limb pulses with blood tests revealing; Hb 101 g/l ESR 87 mm/hr Her symptoms improved following a course of steroids. Which blood vessel is most likely to be affected by her condition?
options: Arteries of the hands and feet
explanation:
Aorta
Takayasu's arteritis is an obliterative arteritis affecting the aorta. Takayasu's arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis typically affecting the aorta and leads to absent limb pulses.

Arteries of the hands and feet
Arteries of the hands and feet - characteristic of Buerger disease

Inferior vena cava (IVC)
IVC and SVC - involved in venous return and do not belong to the arterial system

Superior vena cava (SVC)
IVC and SVC - involved in venous return and do not belong to the arterial system

Renal arteries
Renal arteries - a medium-sized vessel.

stem: A 72-year-old woman who takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension is admitted to the Emergency Department. Admission bloods show the following: Na+ 131 mmol/l K+ 2.2 mmol/l Urea 3.1 mmol/l Creatinine 56 µmol/l Glucose 4.3 mmol/l Which one of the following ECG features is most likely to be seen?
explanation:
U waves
Hypokalaemia - U waves on ECG

J waves
J waves are seen in hypothermia.

stem: You are reviewing a 56-year-old man who has recently been successfully cardioverted following an episode of ventricular tachycardia. He had recently been treated with a course of erythromycin. You are interested to see if he has an underlying prolonged QT interval. What is the most appropriate way to measure the QT interval on the ECG?
options: Time between the end of the Q wave and the start of the T wave
Time between the start of the Q wave and the end of the T wave
Time between the end of the QRS waveform and the start of the T wave
Time between the end of the Q wave and the end of the T wave
Time between the start of the Q wave and the start of the T wave
explanation:
Time between the start of the Q wave and the end of the T wave
QT interval: Time between the start of the Q wave and the end of the T wave.

stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted to the cardiology ward after presenting with fever, malaise and a new murmur. An echocardiogram has shown a vegetation on the aortic valve. Blood cultures are reported as follows: Streptococcus sanguinis isolated What is the most appropriate follow-up given the blood culture results?
options: High resolution CT of the chest
explanation:
Dental review
Patients with very poor dental hygiene may develop endocarditis secondary to Viridans streptococci e.g. Streptococcus sanguinis. Streptococcus sanguinis is one of the viridans group streptococci, or α-hemolytic streptococci, which are common causes of infective endocarditis. They are commensal in the mouth and invasive infection is associated with dental disease. The American Heart Association recommend: 'A thorough dental evaluation should be obtained and all active sources of oral infection should be eradicated.'.

stem: Which of the following statements concerning the third heart sound is correct?
options: Caused by systolic filling of the ventricle
May be heard in constrictive pericarditis
Is characteristically soft in aortic stenosis
Caused by atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
explanation:
May be heard in constrictive pericarditis
Third heart sound - constrictive pericarditis A third heart sound is often heard in left ventricular failure and constrictive pericarditis.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with a deep vein thrombosis in the third trimester of pregnancy. Whilst in the Emergency Department she develops a left hemiparesis. What underlying cardiac abnormality is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Patent foramen ovale
Whilst atrial septal defects may allow emboli to pass from the right side of the heart to the left side, the most common cause is a patent foramen ovale.

stem: A 25-year-old female is found to have a left hemiparesis following a deep vein thrombosis. An ECG shows RBBB with right axis deviation. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Ostium secundum atrial septal defect
The ostium secundum in this patient has allowed passage of an embolus from the right-sided circulation to the left causing a stroke.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred from the Emergency Department with a pulse of 40 beats/min. Which one of the following factors carries the least risk of asystole when risk stratifying the patient?
options: Complete heart block with a narrow complex QRS
Complete heart block with a broad complex QRS
explanation:
Complete heart block with a narrow complex QRS
Complete heart block with a narrow complex QRS complex carries the least risk of asystole as the atrioventricular junctional pacemaker may provide an haemodynamically acceptable and stable heart rate.

The other four factors are indications for transvenous pacing

Recent asystole
The other four factors are indications for transvenous pacing

The other four factors are indications for transvenous pacing

Complete heart block with a broad complex QRS

stem: A 13-year-old male immigrant from India presents to his primary care physician with a gradually worsening shortness of breath worse on physical exertion as well as widespread joint pain. His past medical history includes a severe throat infection which was untreated. His vaccination record is complete. On physical examination, there is a highpitch holosystolic murmur loudest at the apex with radiation to the axilla. Hb 135 g/l Platelets 150 * 109/l WBC 9.5 * 109/l Anti-streptolysin O titres >200units/mL What is the most likely histological finding in his heart?
explanation:
Aschoff bodies
Aschoff bodies are granulomatous nodules found in rheumatic heart fever. This patient has rheumatic heart disease. Mitral valve is the most common valve to be affected. ASO titre indicates exposure to group A streptococcus bacteria. Aschoff bodies (granuloma with giant cells) and Anitschkow cells (enlarged macrophages with ovoid, wavy, rod-like nucleus) are seen in rheumatic heart disease.

Councilman bodies -> hepatitis C, yellow fever

Mallory bodies
Mallory bodies -> alcoholism (hepatocytes)

Schiller-Duval bodies

stem: A 54-year-old man with angina has a percutaneous coronary intervention with insertion of a drug-eluting stent. What is the single most important risk factor for stent thrombosis?
options: Failing to adhere to cardiac rehabilitation program
explanation:
Premature withdrawal of antiplatelet therapy
PCI: stent thrombosis - withdrawal of antiplatelets biggest risk factor

History of diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for restenosis rather than stent thrombosis.

stem: Which one of the following is the most common underlying mechanism causing prolongation of the QT segment?
explanation:
Blockage of potassium channels
Long QT syndrome - usually due to loss-of-function/blockage of K+ channels In long QT syndrome QT prolongation is due to overload of myocardial cells with positively charged ions during ventricular repolarisation. Around 90-95% of inherited causes are due to defects in potassium channels.

stem: You are asked to urgently review a 61-year-old female on the cardiology ward due to difficulty in breathing. On examination she has a raised JVP with bilateral fine crackles to the mid zones. Blood pressure is 94/60 mmHg and the pulse is 140-150 and irregular. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Urgent synchronised DC cardioversion
Heart failure is one of the adverse signs indicating the need for urgent synchronised DC cardioversion.

stem: Which one of the following clinical signs would best indicate severe calcified aortic stenosis?
explanation:
Displaced apex beat
The apex beat is not normally displaced in aortic stenosis. Displacement would indicate left ventricular dilatation and hence severe disease.

stem: A 17-year-old male is taken to the Emergency Department due to alcohol intoxication. On examination he is noted to be tachycardic with a rate of 140bpm. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation. The following morning he is noted to be in sinus rhythm. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Discharge
Supraventricular arrhythmias secondary to acute alcohol intake are well characterised and have been termed 'holiday heart syndrome'. No specific treatment is required.

stem: A 65-year-old man admitted to the Acute Medical Unit is noted to have cannon 'a' waves of his jugular venous pressure during cardiovascular examination. Which one of the following would not cause this finding?
explanation:
Tricuspid stenosis
Whilst tricuspid stenosis may cause large 'a' waves it does not cause cannon 'a' waves.

stem: Which of the following signs is not associated with the development of Eisenmenger's syndrome in a patient with a ventricular septal defect?
options: Large 'a' waves in jugular venous waveform
explanation:
Worsening of systolic murmur
Eisenmenger's syndrome is characterised by the reversal of the left-right shunt due to pulmonary hypertension. The original murmur may disappear once Eisenmenger's syndrome develops.

stem: A patient who takes bendroflumethiazide is noted to have a potassium of 3.1 mmol/l. What is the main mechanism causing hypokalaemia in patients taking bendroflumethiazide?
options: Decreased flow rate in the nephron resulting in a decreased potassium gradient
Increased sodium reaching the collecting ducts
Inhibition of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system secondary to hypovolaemia
Decreased sodium reaching the distal convoluted tubule
Opening of potassium channel in proximal convoluted tubule
explanation:
Increased sodium reaching the collecting ducts
Increased delivery of sodium to the collecting ducts causes the sodium-potassium exchanger to release more potassium into the urine.

Inhibition of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system secondary to hypovolaemia
Another cause is activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system secondary to hypovolaemia.
